Yes, Mr. Speaker, that certainly was in my mind when I made that statement. But perhaps I had better put the full statement on the record, seeing that the right hon. gentleman has quoted part of the paragraph. I was talking about Canada's national purpose, and I quote from the text:
A strong Canadian national purpose rejects, I believe, the idea that the government should forcibly intervene in a labour dispute which has become a lawful strike after the required processes of collective bargaining have been exhausted; intervene, that is, in order to force men back to work.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as I am concerned the answer to the specific question asked by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is no, we have not yet made any protest. I do not think at this particular time any such protest would be helpful. However, he may be assured that we are not very happy about the disclosure of confidential information provided to the United States government, particularly about sales that the Canadian wheat board has made to Japan.
May I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, in view of the question that has been asked, to say just a word about relationships between Canada and the United States in this field?
No.
Mr. Speaker, naturally the hon. gentleman would have to ask to revert to motions so that we would have the opportunity of dealing with and dissecting the statement made.

May I direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. A dispatch from Washington this morning quotes spokesmen of the United States department of agriculture to the effect that on August 6 Canada dropped the price of wheat 6 cents a bushel to coincide with wheat sales to China. It claims that the sale to the U.S.S.R. was at the same price, and that the sale to Japan was at 5 cents below the world price. Will the minister confirm or deny these statements, and will he tell the house whether it is true, as the press report states, that on September 20 Canada assured United States representatives that no further fixed price agreements would be entered into following the wheat deal with the U.S.S.R.?

Mr. Speaker, there are a number of questions asked by the hon. member 28902-5-216J
Inquiries of the Ministry for Burnaby-Coquitlam, and I will see if I can answer them in order. First of all, the Canadian wheat board sells wheat from day to day at the prices that it publishes. The sale to mainland China was made at the published price of the wheat board on that day. So was the sale to the Soviet union, and so was the sale to Japan. As to the suggestion that the price on any of these occasions was below the world market price, I simply do not know what is meant by the question. The Canadian wheat board fixes its sale price from day to day and that is the price, and it sells at that price to all buyers on that day.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. What the report implies is not just that the price to China was 6 cents below the world price but that it was dropped 6 cents below what the board had previously been asking in order to coincide with the agreement. I wonder if the minister would give us some information on that claim.
I think it is well known to all hon. members, Mr. Speaker, that when the sale was made to China the wheat board did reduce its price, and that remained its price until there was a change.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Is there any justifiable reason why the Minister of Trade and Commerce cannot divulge this information to the House of Commons, in view of the fact that the Department of Trade and Commerce and the wheat board have already divulged this information to the general public?
The wheat board never divulges information about its sales contracts.
Everybody knows except us.
The information that was divulged the other day about sales to Japan was not divulged by the wheat board. No announcement was made. I agree with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle that this was a leak.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether it is true that the United States has threatened to launch a trade war against Canada because of Canada's wheat selling practices. Also, perhaps he will clear up the matter if he could tell the house whether or not there have been any previous agreements such as the forward pricing arrangements contained in the recent wheat deal with Japan?

As to the first question, the hon. member knows as much as I do. I have heard no suggestion that there is going to be any

Inquiries of the Ministry trade war between Canada and the United States, and I very much doubt it. As to the second question, whether there have been any other forward sales such as those reported, the answer is yes.

I should like to direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Can he advise the house whether the contracts signed with China and Russia contain provision for price during the duration of those contracts, or whether there would be negotiation as to quantities and prices during the period?

I have explained those transactions on a number of occasions, but in order to refresh the memory of the hon. gentleman, when the contract was entered into by the wheat board for the sale of wheat to mainland China the agreement was for three years. At that time I announced that of the quantity, covered by the agreement, which was a substantial quantity, 500,000 tons had been the subject of a contract on which the price was fixed. In the case of the Soviet union the contract called for delivery within the present crop year and the price was fixed.

I, too, have a supplementary question for the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The hon. gentleman made a statement that the wheat board sold at a fixed price. May I ask him if there is more than one fixed price per day for the wheat board?
My understanding is that the board fixes its price each day and does not vary it during the day. I do not wish to say this is invariably the practice, but it is the practice as I have known it.

Is there any occasion
on which the Department of Trade and Commerce or the wheat board have ever entered into an agreement where there has been a fixed price arrangement for the future?
That is a question for the order paper.

The minister did not reply to the second part of my question. I regret that I was not able to give him notice of my intention to ask it, but the second part of my question was this. On September 20 did representatives of the Canadian government give to representatives of the United States an assurance that following the wheat agreement with the Soviet union no further fixed price agreements would be entered into by Canada?
The answer to that question is no.

Mr. Speaker, my question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been asked over and over again. However, I should like to know if the minister has taken steps to absolve the Canadian wheat board from the accusations of price fixing, and thus protect and encourage the Canadian wheat board?

Mr. Speaker, I think all hon. members know that Canada and the United States are competitors in the wheat markets of the world. They are friendly competitors; nevertheless they are very keen competitors. Each of us is anxious to maintain our business and to get new business. Each of us, I believe, is also very anxious to see some stability in world markets. This is one of the reasons that we are both members of the international wheat agreement, whose purpose is to stabilize world wheat markets. It is under the auspices of the international wheat agreement, and otherwise, that we carry on consultations from time to time with the United States.
Hon. members will recall, for example, that when a joint committee on trade and economic affairs was established many years ago, a committee was established at that time for the very purpose of consulting with one another about wheat policies in order to stabilize the wheat markets of the world. I have no hesitation in saying that this is the purpose of the Canadian government as well as of the Canadian wheat board.
Now, there have been times when our two governments have not seen eye to eye on our respective policies.

May I raise a point of order. I think a suggestion was made earlier that if this matter was going to be discussed it should be done by reverting to motions so the different parties might have an opportunity to present their views.
I am inclined to think the explanation is a bit lengthy; nevertheless there have been a series of questions which tend toward a long answer.
I wonder if the house would give permission to revert to motions? This is a very important matter.
No.

Despite the "no's" from the Liberal side, I understand the minister has a statement prepared on this subject and would be delighted to give it. We asked him about this yesterday, and it is vital to know about the breakdown in the exchange of information between Canada and the United States. I think the minister is prepared to make a statement, and it is vital in view

of the fact a protest has been lodged by the United States government with the Canadian government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as regards the question raised by the hon. member I believe our position to be quite clear. It has been explained in this house time and again, both by the Prime Minister and myself.

subtopic: ST. VINCENT DE PAUL    ASSAULT OF INMATE BY GUARDS
speechtext:
Apart from any other consideration, it so happens that the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi is an intimate personal friend of mine, and I do not think he took any personal offence at all. Then the issue seemed to enter a period of argument, and in order to save the time of the house and to prevent argument about the rulings or suggestions made by the Chair I indicated that the matter was over. I do not think there is much more to add than that. I am sure the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi who, as I have already said, is a personal friend of mine, did not take any personal offence. Certainly none was meant.

subtopic: ST. VINCENT DE PAUL    ASSAULT OF INMATE BY GUARDS

speechtext:

The house resumed from Wednesday, October 9, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. MacEachen-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the placing of the maritime transportation unions of Canada under the management and control of trustees; to provide for the establishment of the board of trustees of the maritime transportation unions consisting of a chairman and two other members; to provide for the payment of their remuneration and expenses and to authorize the employment and remuneration of such personnel as may be necessary for the carrying out of the duties and powers of the trustees under the said measure.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the few minutes which I had yesterday I said that the labour movement in Canada for historical reasons was opposed in principle to the idea of government intervention in the internal business of labour unions; but because of the record of violence and intimidation the executive council of the Canadian Labour Congress, having amongst its members the top officers of Canadian unions both national and international, met this week in Ottawa and reluctantly approved the proposal of the government of Canada to impose a trusteeship on the maritime unions, and particularly on the S.I.U.
It did so because in the opinion of the labour movement the S.I.U. is not a legitimate trade union. The labour movement in Canada is proud of the fact that in nearly every case the unions in Canada are democratic. They are being conducted honestly. They are keeping their members informed about what goes on and getting approval from their members of decisions which are made. The salaries paid to union officers are set by union conventions. Expenses for union business are carefully audited. In the history of the Canadian labour movement there has been little evidence of misuse of funds. Most of the unions in Canada, like the ladies garment workers, the steel workers, the packing house workers, have pioneered, in
Maritime Transportation Unions regular and frequent reports to their membership, the giving of full financial reports.
If we look at the report of Justice Norris we see how differently the affairs of the seafarers international union were conducted. Justice Norris reports that in the course of four years, namely from 1959 to 1962, Mr. Banks had expenses of over $80,000 for which he provided vouchers for just over $8,000. In that period of time Mr. Banks increased the salary paid himself and other top officials of the union without getting the approval of the membership and without reporting it to the members. No legitimate trade union in Canada or the United States would permit such activity and no legitimate trade union leader would be a partner to that. Mr. Justice Norris reports that thousands of dollars of union funds were spent on a lavish apartment for the personal use of Mr. Banks. He also reports that union funds were used for air travel for friends or relatives of Mr. Banks who had nothing to do with the business of the union.
This is not the way for any legitimate trade unionist to act, Mr. Chairman, and it is not surprising therefore that the labour movement has agreed to trusteeship. Mr. Banks was able to keep control of the union by the use of the "do not ship" list, and later by the "report of charges" cards. Thousands of workers were prevented by this method from working, although the whole system was declared illegal by the courts. But the workers knew that if they were put on this list they would lose completely their opportunity to work. Under those circumstances they had no alternative but to take orders from Mr. Banks and his henchmen.
Justice Norris has documented the use of violence and intimidation by the S.I.U. under the direction of Mr. Banks. In schedule 31 of the Norris report there are listed the acts of violence and intimidation, and hon. members ought to read this to see how people were beaten, how others were subjected to telephone harassment. There was the ransacking of offices, damage to property, firing with guns on ships and stoning of vessels. The power of Mr. Banks over the whole industry can be seen very clearly from a letter which a Captain Watson wrote to Mr. Banks and which I want to read into the record. It is to be found at page 208 of the report. It is dated October 7, 1954, and is addressed to Mr. Hal Banks, president, S.I.U., Montreal.
Dear Mr. Banks,
In regards to a letter I wrote about two months ago to the newspaper in Owen Sound, Ontario.
In this letter I made some disparaging remarks about you for which I now tender my sincere and humble apologies.
The main body of the letter I copied from a Toronto newspaper, but have since come to the

Maritime Transportation Unions
conclusion that the write up in the newspaper was an attempt to attack the union, through its leaders, and I was sucked in as probably some others were. However I was foolish enough to go into print with my opinions and must now offer my apology, this along with my avowal to refrain from any comments about you or anybody else is all I can offer to you in the way of reparation.
My job and my family's welfare depend now entirely on your mercy.
I hope you will accept my apology and in your benevolence allow me to keep my job so I can keep my family.
If there is anything I can do to square this with you I will most earnestly do so.
Yours very sincerely
J. M. Watson S.S. George Hindman.
I want to point out that this letter was written on the stationery of the Hindman Transportation Company Limited. Following that letter Justice Norris says, according to page 208 of the report:
Howard Hindman, the president of the company, was cross-examined by commission counsel, and he admitted that as a result of a telephone call from Banks, Captain George Hindman, then head of the company, "suggested" that Watson write the letter. Howard Hindman admitted that Watson "must have been in a frantic state when he wrote a letter like that".
In other words, so great is the power of Mr. Banks that the president of a shipping company with which Mr. Banks does business permits the captain of a ship to write this kind of abject letter. It is no wonder that Mr. Banks felt that he could do virtually anything in this country. Justice Norris has given a very short and descriptive impression of Mr. Banks which I think should be put on the record. He says, as reported at page 249:
Banks is capable, decisive, egocentric, intolerant and ruthless. He is of the stuff of the Capones and the Hoff as of whom the dictators throughout history, from the earliest times to the totalitarians, Hitler and Stalin, are prototypes. He is a bully, cruel, dishonest, greedy, power hungry, contemptuous of the law. In his mouth, the use of the word "democracy" is sheer blasphemy. For him the big lie" and the failure to remember are ever-ready weapons and shields.
Well, Mr. Chairman, Mr. Banks is not by any stretch of the imagination representative of the real labour leaders of this country. It is being suggested by some newspapers and commentators that somehow labour is responsible for Mr. Banks, that all labour should be tarred with the same brush. It is forgotten by many people that it was the C.L.C. which expelled Mr. Banks and the S.I.U. from the ranks of organized labour; that it was the C.L.C. which forced the former government to act on the cancer by closing the seaway. It was the C.L.C. which asked the government to take whatever steps were necessary to clear up the mess. It was the C.L.C. which urged Justice Norris to bring forward any recommendations necessary to [Mr. Orlikow.I
clear up the situation. The C.L.C. has also accepted his report, even though it is in principle opposed to trusteeship. But, Mr. Chairman, no gangster can get power and keep power unless the people he works with co-operate. Labour has acted on its own in so far as it could by expelling the S.I.U. from the labour movement. Mr. Justice Norris has made proposals with respect to controlling the unions in the industry and we are now being asked to act upon them. But despite the fact that Mr. Justice Norris has some very scathing things to say about the companies in the industry, we have not yet had any suggestion by the government that steps will be taken to apply the same kind of sanctions against the companies as will be applied against the unions concerned.
I think it should be of interest to the public to know something about the industry, and particularly about the largest company in the industry which Mr. Justice Norris has blamed for being responsible for the difficulties to a great extent, and for permitting Mr. Banks to continue as he did. I want to put on the record the names of some of the distinguished, shall I call them, directors of Canada Steamship Lines Limited. This information can be found in the directory of directors issued by the Financial Post. The president is T. R. McLagan and the vice president is H. A. Cresswell. The directors are D. W. Ambridge, G. C. Bateman, Hon. T. A. Crerar, J. H. Davey, A. O. Dufresne, Sir Philip Dunn, D. S. Holbrook, W. H. Howard, J. A. Mathewson, Gordon McMillan, K. A. Powell, R. W. Milner, H. A. Cresswell and T. R. McLagan.
Let us look at these people, because they are not only directors of Canada Steamship Lines. Mr. McLagan, besides being president and general manager of Canada Steamship Lines, is a director and member of the executive committee of the Algoma Steel Corporation, a director of Abitibi Power and Paper Company, British Petroleum Canada Limited, Canadair Limited, the Foundation Company of Quebec Limited and the Royal Bank of Canada.
Mr. Cresswell, besides being a director of Canada Steamship Lines, is vice president and director of Century Coal Company Limited and a director of Reliance Insurance Company. Mr. Ambridge, besides being a director of Canada Steamship Lines, is president of Abitibi Power and Paper Company Limited and a director of Canadian Petrofina Limited, the Montreal Trust Company and the Royal Bank of Canada. Hon. T. A. Crerar, besides being a senator and a director of Canada Steamship Lines, is chairman of the advisory committee of the Eastern Trust Company and a director of the Great West Life

Assurance Company. Mr. Dufresne is a director of Noranda Mines Limited and of Gaspe Copper Mines Limited. Mr. Holbrook is president and chairman of the Algoma Steel Corporation and a director of the Royal Bank of Canada.
I could go on and on, Mr. Chairman, but it is obvious that these people between them constitute a veritable who's who of Canadian business. I suggest they have some responsibility, and I want to put on the record some of the activities of the top officials who work for them, because their role in this sordid story is really an infamous one. Mr. Dunker-ley, the personnel manager of Canada Steamship Lines in charge of labour relations, is in my opinion a disgrace to legitimate business. He ignored the law. He conspired with Mr. Banks.
For members who may question my characterization of him, let me read from the report presented by Mr. Justice Norris. I quote from page 54:
In February of 1959, Dunkerley, personnel manager of the C.S.L. in charge of labour relations, advised Greaves that the C.S.L. had signed a collective agreement with the S.I.U. licensed division in spite of the fact that that company had a collective bargaining agreement with N.A.M.E. Greaves testified that when he pointed out to Dunkerley that the action of the C.S.L. in signing an agreement with the S.I.U. was illegal, Dunkerley said:
"Did you read the statement I made a couple of days ago before our management associations? There are no teeth in the labour laws. Have a look at the act. First of all you have to go to the minister and get permission to prosecute. That will take you a couple of months. We will kick it around in the courts here for a year and if necessary we will take it to the Supreme Court of Canada. This will take about two years."
Greaves swore that Dunkerley told him that there would be merely a fine if the company was found guilty.
"We have assurance from Mr. Banks of indemni-".cation. By this time you will be out of business if you do not get your dues coming in, you know that. That is the way of life."
I suggest this is conspiracy. Some time ago I put a question on the order paper asking whether the government was considering the prosecution of the officials of the company concerned. It may be that the directors whom I have mentioned did not bother with the day to day operations of the company and did not know the kind of operation Mr. Dunkerley was conducting, but surely they knew about it after the Norris report came out. But still there is no action against Mr. Dunkerley. I presume that if he comes to Ottawa he will be a welcome guest at the Rideau club, along with all the other members of the establishment who are welcome there.
It is a sad state of affairs when you look at the principles on which businessmen are
Maritime Transportation Unions basing their operations. What about the business ethics of Canada Steamship Lines? Let us turn to the Norris report again. On pages 142 and 143 there is a fantastic story by Mr. Banks in which he claims that Canada Steamship Lines, this great organization directed by some of the greatest and wealthiest businessmen in the country, had a plan to transfer their whole Canadian operations from Canada to Bermuda. Why? So they could get out of paying the legitimate income taxes which they would have to pay in this country.
Mr. Banks has been called a lot of things and he may have been lying on this occasion, but it is significant that Canada Steamship Lines did not take occasion, as I am sure they would have if Mr. Banks had been lying or exaggerating, to ask for the right to appear before Mr. Justice Norris to deny the story which Mr. Banks put on the record. Therefore I have to assume that this is an honest statement and that this is what their intentions were. The fact that they did not go through with it is a separate matter, but these are the kind of people who are running one of the biggest companies in an important Canadian industry.
Banks has been expelled from the labour movement but Mr. Dunkerley remains as a top official of Canada Steamship Lines. Mr. Banks' union is being put under trusteeship, or will be as soon as the legislation proposed is passed by parliament, I assume. I hope that one of the first steps the trustees will take will be to see that Mr. Banks is fired as head of the S.I.U. and that he no longer has any position or influence in the Canadian branch of the S.I.U.
What about Canada Steamship Lines? What about Mr. Dunkerley? No action has yet been proposed. To some of us, Mr. Chairman, it looks like we have one law for labour misdeeds and another law for management misdeeds, in fact, no law for management misdeeds, which makes it even worse. If we can devise a law to put the union under trusteeship, surely the very competent lawyers and other technical people in the Department of Labour and Department of Justice could devise amendments to laws such as the Canada Shipping Act, so that companies and their officers who break Canadian laws will be penalized.
But nothing has been suggested, Mr. Chairman. I for one wonder why. I think the Minister of Labour should give us the reasons why there has been no suggestion of any move on the part of the government to punish companies, which are just as guilty of offences against the Canadian people and against the law as are Mr. Banks and the S.I.U.

Maritime Transportation Unions
But, Mr. Chairman, we need not have waited until 1963 to act in this matter. We have heard a great deal from the former prime minister and the former minister of labour about the friendship of Mr. Banks for the Liberal party. I believe that has been and can be documented. However, it is not my intention to add to that criticism. The members of the Liberal government will have to answer for that themselves. The former government had an opportunity to act in this connection.
In 1959, Mr. Bernard Wilson, the director of industrial relations, Department of Labour, received a letter from Mr. Misener of Scott Misener Steamships Limited. I believe this letter has already been read into the record on several occasions. In this letter Mr. Misener informed Mr. Wilson that, despite an agreement which his company had with another union which had been certified, his company proposed to ignore the certification and signed an agreement with Mr. Banks' union. Along with that letter, there was a copy of a letter from Mr. Banks guaranteeing the company's indemnification if they were sued for damages.
Now, Mr. Chairman, Mr. Wilson's reputation is well known in the Canadian labour movement. I cannot believe for one moment that Mr. Wilson did not consider that a violation of the Canada labour relations act was a serious offence. I cannot believe for a moment that Mr. Wilson did not report this case to the former minister of labour or that the former minister of labour did not report the matter to the then prime minister. We have to ask ourselves, therefore, why the former government did not prosecute the company and the S.I.U. at that time. Had they done that, Mr. Chairman, in all likelihood, we would not be faced with the problems with which we are now faced. We have a right to ask what pressures were brought upon the former government, and by whom. We can only speculate on this, although there are some rather interesting rumors in this connection.
It is certain, too, that the procrastination of the former government, as well as the failure of the Liberal government to deport Mr. Banks when they had not only the right but the obligation to do so, has cost us dearly and has contributed to the condition on the great lakes. We need to take action to clean up this unholy mess. While we are taking action we need to make certain that all the guilty people are punished, whether they are the so-called labour leaders like Mr. Banks, or business leaders, whether they be Mr. McLagan, Mr. Dunkerley, Senator Crerar or

anybody else. No matter who they are, what their power or influence, all of them should be brought to justice.
I should like to conclude by saying that we in this group are, in principle, opposed to government interference with the free labour movement. We do not like, we deplore, the necessity for this legislation. We deplore the idea of trusteeship. We think that five years is too long. However, we are prepared to accept this legislation. We are prepared to support this legislation. We are prepared to go back to our people, to the labour movement with whom we have a close connection, and to explain the necessity for this. But, Mr. Chair-man, I want to say to the Minister of Labour and to the Minister of Justice that it would be a lot easier to explain if we could tell the labour movement at the same time that the people on the other side who are just as guilty, but who may have a little more influence, will also be punished.

Mr. Chairman, in so far as the allegations that were made in the penultimate paragraph of the hon. gentleman's speech, they will be answered by the hon. member for Ontario who will show conclusively that the action taken by the former government went as far as it could go under the circumstances, and in no way was dictated by any other consideration than that the law be administered equally and fairly. He will deal with that phase.
I rise, however, this afternoon to add something to the stand that was taken on behalf of the official opposition by the former minister of labour. I begin by pointing out the fact that while parliament is in session we have been endeavouring for a number of days to secure a declaration of policy from the government relative to the longshoremen's strike which, as I stated the other day, is connected very directly with the lack of action by the government to bring about trusteeship in the latter part of July. While we have waited for a declaration of policy in this regard, the Canadian Club in the city of Toronto received information that has been denied consistently to parliament.
I said a moment ago that I was going to deal with one or two phases of this matter which, as yet, have not received the attention of the house. Hon. members in all parties are agreed that this type of extraordinary legislation ought not to be passed except when the circumstances deny any other available course of action in the national interest. Ever since the Norris commission made its report, there has been a continuing series of disorders on the great lakes. The Norris report was clear and unequivocal. I say this, that what is taking place at this very moment on

the St. Lawrence river is directly attributable to, or indirectly the result of the failure of this government to act on the Norris report when it should have acted, that is, before the adjournment of this house in the month of August.

The hon. gentleman can deny it. I am going to refer to the arrival of a distinguished United States labour representative by the name of Gleason, the head of a union organization. I am going to refer to the degree to which throughout the years he and Mr. Banks have co-operated in illegal action, in intimidation, in international blackmail. Now, we find ourselves, as a result of the failure of the government to act, in a very dangerous situation economically in this nation.
There has been, as I said a moment ago, a long record of association between the longshoremen's union and the S.I.U. Today we face a situation on the St. Lawrence which, in my opinion, would be nonexistent if the government had acted as it should have, instead of adopting the attitude of indolence that has characterized it throughout the problem.
Nobody opposed the trusteeship, and in this connection I shall refer to the attitude of the great labour leaders of our country. They certainly did not welcome it as something they would like to have as a regular course of action; but recognizing and realizing something had to be done, and that the recommendation made by Mr. Justice Norris met the demands of the moment and the needs of the preservation of free international and national trade union rights, they admitted there was no other course available.
But what happened? The government played around with the problem as it has played around with others. The great labour leaders in Canada were prepared to accept this trusteeship, but the government stalled.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, one thinks of the cuckoo in June when those interruptions are made. I point out that Banks had an unchallengeable position and no denial can take place. Regarding the order in council, they hid Banks' record, and hid his conviction for being in possession of smuggled goods. They gave him the status of a man who was above challenge, so long as thereafter he lived within the law. Over and over again we had this looked into, to see whether after that order in council-and following the change in the law which took place in June 1952, a measure introduced as I recall by Mr. Harris-there were any means whereby we could do anything to Banks; but he was above the law.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES

He enjoyed an unchallengeable position, and now we have the delay, postponement, procrastination, indecision and confusion that have been the position of the government since the month of July. Why was there this delay? It was because the

government had an irresistible urge to seek a way out. It did not want to act.
The government could not blame our great trade union leaders. Mr. Jodoin, president of the Canadian Labour Congress, came out publicly in favour of the trusteeship. Mr. Smith of the Canadian brotherhood of railway and transportation workers supported it. No single voice of Canadian labour opposed it. All realized there was no other way of breaking the hold and the power of Banks.
The other day the minister said he was waiting because he believed in clean, democratic trade unionism. So do we. Does the minister say that clean, democratic trade unionism is unknown to Mr. Jodoin, Mr. Dodge, Mr. Smith and the other leaders who agreed to accept the trusteeship? However the government did not act. It had to see all these various people.
Mr. Jodoin, to his credit, remained firm. He did not welcome this kind of legislation but he realized the need for action being taken. Canadian labour refused to accept any kind of a cooked up deal that would have left Harold Chamberlain Banks in command of the Canadian seamen on great lakes. I say if Canadian labour leaders never do any more than they did on this occasion in connection with this matter, in standing firm in the interests of Canadians, they will do well for those they represent. But the government stalled, and I repeat what I said the other day, even though it has been denied, that what is happening today in Montreal is in fact in keeping with what one would expect would take place, if there is any co-operation as between Mr. Gleason and Mr. Banks. Mr. Gleason has just arrived in Montreal. What is he there for? He comes over from the United States. Has he been working in the past with Mr. Banks? Is the past past, and does he no longer work with him? The hon. gentleman who preceded me read from the record. I intend to do so also. On page 276 we read this:
The position of the M.T.D. and particularly of its international division has been dealt with. It is well to consider now the other organizations which are supporting the activities of Banks, the S.I.U. and the M.T.D., in the harassment of upper lakes vessels and in the interference with international and interprovincial trade.
The president of the teamsters is James R. Hoffa.
Then he says on page 277:
The president of this association-
Mr. Justice Norris is referring to the international longshoremen's association:
-is William V. Bradley; its general organizer is Thomas Gleason. These two have been closely associated with Banks.
Now I want to quote what Mr. Meany said about Mr. Gleason. He is the man behind the

man behind the strike on the St. Lawrence. Mr. Justice Norris says on page 278:
On November 19, 1953, a statement was issued by George Meany at the conclusion of a meeting of the board of trustees supervising the new international longshoremen's association:
"The racketeers who are trying to perpetuate their control of the port of New York failed in their attempt yesterday to camouflage their 'front' organization with a new look''.
Then he goes on to say:
"He exposed''-
This is referring to Bradley:
-"the true nature of his supporters when he credited his election''-
That is, the election of the new president: -"to the work of Thomas Gleason, a local union official who was cited in testimony before the New York state crime investigating committee for consorting with gangsters and accepting gratuities from stevedoring and steamship company officials.
"The actions at Philadelphia add up to one inescapable conclusion-the mob is still in complete control of the old I.L.A."
Then Mr. Justice Norris goes on to say:
It is to be noted what Mr. Meany said about Bradley and Gleason in this statement-the same Bradley and Gleason who now control the affairs of the I.L.A. and at the present time are assisting Banks in his lawless acts.
It was back in June or July when Mr. Justice Norris wrote this, that this man Gleason, who is now in Montreal, the head of the I.L.A., had assisted Banks in his lawless acts. Then he goes on to say:
The violence and excesses which existed in the operations of the I.L.A. under Bradley and Gleason and in the operations of the teamsters under Hoffa, are of a pattern with the acts of lawlessness which have occurred during Banks' regime and in connection with the dispute with Upper Lakes.
Bradley and Gleason of the I.L.A. and Hoffa's teamsters are the people who have, with the S.I.U. of North America, been assisting Banks to maintain absolute power on the great lakes.
There is the record. This is the man, Gleason, who now comes into our midst. This is the man who is going to see what can be done. Again I come back to what I have said on previous occasions, that what is happening in Montreal has a direct connection with Banks and his opposition to a trusteeship and the maintenance of law and order in this country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I go on to say this. The judge dealt with Banks, Gleason and Hoffa. What a triumvirate of lawlessness got together there. Hoffa, Gleason and Banks are together, dominating Canada, challenging parliament. The other day one of them said, "If the minister tells us to go back to work, we will not go. If parliament tells us to go back to work, we will go back but we will not work". What anarchy is this that they
Maritime Transportation Unions would perpetrate upon the Canadian people? Who are these demi-gods? Then Mr. Justice Norris concluded in this way:
The fact that these are the elements that are actively working together today as a federation, but lacking only the formalities of organization, in an effort to maintain a one-man lawless rule over shipping on the great lakes, is a threat to our democracy of the gravest kind.
There you have it. Here we have the I.L.A., with Gleason arriving in Montreal to see what he can do. The I.L.A. and Gleason are united with Banks, according to Mr. Justice Norris. No wonder men like Mr. Jodoin and other outstanding labour leaders have said that this action of appointing a trusteeship, while it is not something they would accept with alacrity, is something that must be accepted in the interests of the nation as a whole. I simply wanted to place this on the record because this triumvirate have been together before. I ask the committee to look at the Montreal Star of November 20, 1960. It is very interesting that on the left of the picture you have Thomas Gleason with Hal Banks having his arm around him in affectionate embrace.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
You begin to see the connection. Canada's economy is challenged by this type of person, Gleason and those associated with him; a man who has been guilty of lawlessness, in association with gangsters and in co-operation with Banks. That is why the problem that faces the government has been one of great difficulty. I repeat what I said earlier, that if the government had acted and given parliament the opportunity to appoint the trusteeship in early August before we adjourned, these things that are happening now, the challenge to the economy of the country, which denies people the right to travel here and there on the St. Lawrence, would not have taken place. Just imagine: this is 1963, and the Canadian weekly newspapers association people returning, together with the others who are with them, cannot get off a ship; they are imprisoned there by the lawlessness of the Gleasons who in the past have been the company and the associates of the Banks.
There you see the whole picture-Banks fighting against a trusteeship which will dethrone him from his arrogant position today of dominating above the law those that come under his control, and his friend Gleason arriving in Montreal to see what can be done. When Gleason was asked what he came for, he stated as follows, as reported in today's Globe and Mail:
Thomas Gleason, president of the international longshoremen's association, flew here from New York to have a look at the situation and to confer with the strikers.

Maritime Transportation Unions
While the government delayed and refused to face the situation, the tremendous volume of opposition to action set the scene for the mobilization of the Gleasons and those associated with them in an endeavour to defy parliament and the Canadian people.
I did not hear this broadcast last evening but I am informed that it took place. President Assslin of the international longshoremen in Montreal told a C.B.C. reporter that his union was friendly to the seafarers' international union. This was in answer to a direct question, whether the longshoremen's strike was being undertaken to bring pressure on the government to counter the imposition of the trusteeship. The reply he gave was, as I have said, that his union was very friendly to the S.I.U.
A moment ago I mentioned some of the operations of these people. In 1949, through 1950 and 1951, Banks coerced various great lakes companies to sign contracts. He did so by blocking United States ports such as Detroit against Canadian vessels importing newsprint or iron ore. He was able to do so by enlisting the support of the international longshoremen's association whose members, together with those of other waterfront unions in United States ports, would refuse to cross picket lines established by the S.I.U.
I think we are unanimous in support of the legislation which this government has introduced. I want to thank the minister for the explanation he gave in detail before this measure was presented. He mentioned a period of five years. I think that period could well be reduced to two years. But the principle, as I say, we support. We are in condemnation of the government for their failure to act courageously in July and August. We condemn them for following, as they did, a course of waiting, hoping, anticipating-doing everything but face the situation until circumstances took over and they were forced to act.

speechtext:
Having had a long and close association with trade unions, I am anxious to express my views on certain aspects of this matter. First, let me say I was startled to hear the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition. I thought there was a flavour of Alice in Wonderland attached to them. I could hardly believe my ears when the right hon. gentleman who headed the previous administration had the unmitigated gall to criticize my hon. friend the Minister of Labour for not having acted more promptly in this matter, when the whole problem of strife on the great lakes arose solely as a result of the prolonged procrastination of the former administration.
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
A similar degree of procrastination has not been seen before. Though the situation on the great lakes was deteriorating steadily, nothing was done about it by the previous administration. I should have thought the Leader of the Opposition would have slouched low in his seat during the course of this debate and have taken no part in it at all. The hon. member for Red Deer suggested that the former administration had turned a blind eye toward the growing strife on the great lakes in 1961 and 1962. I suggest they turned two blind eyes toward this problem. How much, I ask the committee, did the power of Mr. Banks grow during the six years when the former administration was in power? How far did the tentacles of this octopus spread during all the years when the previous administration sat back and did nothing? Let me go further and say, as regards the feeble effort made by the right hon. gentleman this afternoon to find some connection between the strike presently under way in Montreal and the great lakes situation involving the S.I.U., that never since the miracle of the loaves and fishes has so much been made out of so little. We have the international president of a union which is holding a legal strike in Montreal visiting the city where this serious strike is under way. Out of this act alone, the Leader of the Opposition would conclude that there was a deep and dark conspiracy involving the tie-in of the two strikes. Certainly, this is a defence mechanism of the worst type, set up in order to avoid the blame which lies naturally on the shoulders of the former administration for allowing Banks and his power to grow and grow while they sat and sat and did nothing.
It is my intention to support this legislation establishing a public trusteeship over the maritime unions, but I did not reach such a conclusion as quickly as did some members of the official opposition. As a matter of fact, I did not reach it with the alacrity of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam who, as early as July, urged that the government press ahead with trusteeship legislation and advised it not to consider any alternative remedies.
So alien is the prospect of a government trusteeship over trade unions, in my philosophy of labour and concept of democracy, that I could not bring myself to support this legislation until all possibility of an effective alternative remedy had vanished. Even now, I support it, not with a glad heart, but with the knowledge that this incursion into the freedom of association of workers in our country and into their freedom to manage their own affairs must be reluctantly accepted in order to protect the greater and

more basic rights of those workers and, indeed, of all citizens, in order that they may carry on their lawful activities without intimidation, violence and corruption permeating those activities.
I sincerely hope that no province in Canada will consider this action by the federal parliament as a precedent to be followed in the future. I hope this parliament itself will not consider the action we now propose as a precedent except in a most serious situation such as we face at this time. My reservations concerning this legislation were heightened by a conviction that the trusteeship legislation proposed is not a cure-all and, indeed, that it may wholly fail to rectify the evils that exist. Nevertheless, with the proper support of parliament, the public and the seamen, it may succeed, provided a wise choice of trustees is made and, therefore, it must be attempted.
I would in part agree with the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Red Deer who suggested that our federal labour laws need to be overhauled. Though I am sure I would disagree with some of the specific changes the hon. member might wish to make, it must be recognized that the growth of lawlessness and tyranny within the ranks of the S.I.U. was only possible because of the inadequacies of our labour laws. We must remove the inadequacies which allow such a situation to develop by bringing in new legislation, but legislation which still assures the independence and freedom of our trade associations.
Our outdated labour legislation recognizes no difference between industrial plant type operations and far reaching transportation activities. The hon. member for Red Deer, in speaking on this legislation, was extremely critical of the closed shop as a weapon by which the S.I.U. were able to impose their wholly unreasonable control on the livelihoods of so many sailors. I gather from the context of his remarks that he feels the closed shop should be outlawed. I would agree with the hon. member that there might be some merit in substituting a union shop arrangement for a closed shop for certain sea-going commercial activities, because this would remove the power of assignment from the S.I.U. union bosses and enable the company to determine what seamen they would employ subject, of course, to seniority provisions on recall and the provision that new employees would be required to join the union within a specified time. But the danger of generalization of the type indulged in by the hon. member, and further evidence of the need for legislation with varying provisions for different types of industrial activities is found in the fact that the closed shop
Maritime Transportation Unions has worked very satisfactorily in the construction industry, and it is indeed hard to conceive how the interests of the workers in that industry could be properly protected without closed shop provisions. I would hope that as soon as this trusteeship is firmly established the government would consider the legislation that is necessary to prevent the development of a similar situation in the emergence of another Hal Banks in some other union. I hope that the government will in time consider the possibility of other legislation, such as an examination of pension and welfare funds by a committee of the labour relations board, and review the amount of initiation fees and dues paid to the unions to determine whether they are realistic or for the purposes of keeping people out. I think that the whole role of the labour relations board should be reviewed, at all times keeping in mind that the independence of the trade unions must be protected.
While we in Canada admire much about our great neighbour to the south, I for one have anything but admiration for the lawless type of gangsterism within certain trade unions in that nation, and the seeming inability of the United States administration and courts to curtail such trends. We in Canada must here and now show that we have the legislative courage and the administrative ability to guarantee the workers of our nation that trade unions shall be operated for the benefit of the members and not for the enrichment of unprincipled, dictatorial leaders. If we are successful in reestablishing democratic trade unionism on the great lakes, then we shall have conclusively demonstrated to any other prospective gangster union czar that Canada is not fertile soil for this type of activity.
I note from the newspaper reports that the action of this parliament in establishing a trusteeship will not be accepted in good grace by United States labour leaders, and there are reports that the continuation of the export of this whole national matter may be marked by further harassment of Canadian shipping in U.S. ports. I sincerely hope that this will not be the case. Unfortunately, some United States union leaders seem more concerned with retaining membership in their operations than in distinguishing right from wrong. I would say, as a private member, for the benefit of these leaders, that continued interference in this wholly Canadian matter by United States union interests after parliament has acted would be most unwise. I feel that private members on all sides of this house, with the support of public opinion would, in these circumstances, press for a greater degree of autonomy for the Canadian branches of

Maritime Transportation Unions U.S.-based international unions, and I suggest there is a good possibility that legislation could follow. While United States unions financed and greatly speeded the organization of Canadian workers in the early years, the Canadian trade union movement has now reached a maturity sufficient to allow it to stand on its own feet, and if United States unions are to interfere in our disputes and continue to refuse to recognize our national existence as an independent state, then they may find that they are providing the catalyst for the early development of a wholly independent Canadian trade union movement.
Some officials of the United States government have been critical of our government's announced intention to proceed with this legislation. However, they make no realistic or constructive suggestion as to how they would handle a similar situation. Having observed their inability to curtail the Hoffas, one can only conclude that they are hardly experts in dealing with such situations. I feel, however, that the United States has a legitimate interest in this dispute, as the St. Lawrence seaway is an international commission and much great lakes shipping takes place between our two countries. So I am not sure that the United States government can be criticized, as it was by one speaker, for expressing its views on our proposed legislation, although I am not at all sure that they would willingly accept our criticism of lawlessness in their unions, which is of concern in this country because of international trade union affiliation.
Every praise should be given to the Minister of Labour for the manner in which he has dealt with this perplexing problem. Every praise should be given to him because he has exhausted every more palatable choice before introducing this trusteeship legislation. He acted in a forthright manner in all his dealings with those concerned, and I suggest he discharged the duties of the Minister of Labour in an outstanding manner at a time of unprecedented labour problems.
I should like, Mr. Chairman, to say a word or two on the question of the five-year term. The length of time of the appointment of the trusteeship has been criticized to some degree. I too would hope that there would be no necessity for this trusteeship to last a full five years; but I suggest that it is better that the trusteeship be set for the longer period of time, with every hope and expectation that it will be possible to dissolve the trusteeship before that time. Far better to do that than to have to get a further extension, should the situation not improve in a short period. I think the five-year term is an unduly long time, but I think it was set as an outside

limit with every hope and expectation that the trusteeship will be concluded long before that time.
I should like to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam as regards the personnel to make up the trustees. I think they should be chosen with great care. I think they should be men who have had a thorough knowledge both of management and of labour. If we follow this trusteeship with legislation making our unions less attractive prey for gangster elements, then a great service will have been done the nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to support the need for government action, extraordinary action to deal with an extraordinary situation. The problem of the Canadian seamen manning the ships on the great lakes has had public attention focused on it many times during the past 20 years. I think the sorry situation we have to deal with today
ever, I suppose it is easy to be wise in retrospect.
I do not intend, Mr. Chairman, to review all of the rivalry between the various seamen's unions because this rivalry, this raiding and what may even be termed war between the various seamen's unions, has been spelled out rather well in the Norris report. Furthermore, it has been discussed by many members preceding me in the debate.
I believe that setting up a trusteeship is one of the first essential steps that will be necessary to deal with a situation that has been festering for all these years. But, Mr. Chairman, I am also convinced that unless the government and particularly the Department of Justice are prepared to enforce the law of the land, even this trusteeship will fail in its desired objective. Had there been reasonably strict enforcement of the law of the land, those laws that give protection to life, liberty and freedom of individuals as Canadian citizens, whether they be engaged in the maritime shipping industry or any other occupation, the situation we have to deal with now would not have developed.
The Minister of Labour, in his opening remarks when introducing the resolution, stated that the government waited; that is to say, they delayed bringing in this bill to give an opportunity for some kind of interunion arrangement, which might have been a solution preferable to action by parliament providing for a public trusteeship. We may be able to agree that some delay was justified for that purpose, but I cannot agree that any delay is justified in enforcing those laws that are necessary to protect all Canadian citizens from intimidation and beatings or which are designed to preserve human dignity.
I should like to ask the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Justice for an explanation why the law enforcement officers of this country have not been ordered to take appropriate action when there is official testimony contained in the Norris report that Canadian citizens have been attacked, have been beaten and have been intimidated repeatedly. I could refer to a lot of documents, statements in the press and statements by various labour unions that have drawn to the attention of the government and the law enforcement agencies that this has been going on. We have repeatedly asked the Minister of Justice what he is prepared to do about it, but even as late as this afternoon he told us he is still studying an interim report which he has.
From the issue of Maclean's magazine of May 18 last I should like to quote the following:
A man who wants to sail on a Canadian lake-ship faces more than the domination Banks exerts

Maritime Transportation Unions through ROC cards and other weapons within his own union. He faces the chance, if the joins the Canadian Maritime Union, the only other union that is now open to him, of getting his head beaten in. Witness after witness at the Norris commission testified about terrible beatings. One of them appeared on the stand in August still wearing a cast from a beating suffered in April. At least one appeared still woozy. Some of them had been beaten by as as many as seven men. Some had been struck by baseball bats. One had been nearly killed on his own front lawn. The victims included women.
As Norris himself said after only 12 days of testimony: "Without at all at this time deciding who is responsible for these attacks, these cowardly attacks, it is very difficult for me to understand how in this state of our so-called civilization things of this sort could happen in Canada. We have heard, day after day, witnesses coming here and telling us of these most cowardly attacks. That is why I referred to them as a pack of jackals."
The magazine article continues:
In all the 107 days of hearings, no one ever proved that the beatings were inflicted by the S.I.U. Certainly Banks, the central figure, was never even accused of being directly involved.
This is the most important sentence, Mr. Chairman.
Yet all the victims of the beatings had one thing in common: they opposed the S.I.U.
I do not want to take the time now but I should like to refer hon. members, if they have not already read it, to the evidence contained in the schedules that were submitted by Mr. Justice Norris. Schedule 31 gives details of the beatings, and the interesting thing is that in the right hand column of the schedule which indicates the action taken, if any, there is very little indication that the law enforcement officers tried to protect these people from these attacks, nor did they try to apprehend the people who were doing the attacking. So, Mr. Chairman, as I have said before, I think that the enforcement of the law, whether or not we set up a trusteeship, is by far the most important aspect, t believe that the main reason this situation has deteriorated to the point it has today is the lack of law enforcement. I want to emphasize that law enforcement to protect Canadian citizens against this kind of treatment is not confined to seamen's unions or to the difficulties connected with labour unions. It is, rather, a universal right of all citizens, whether they be part of the labour union movement or not.
Indeed, the right of a citizen to protection from this kind of lawlessness by the full strength of the law enforcement agencies is spelled out in some Canadian statutes. I refer, for example, to the bill of rights, which is an act of this parliament. We all know, Mr. Chairman, it was one of the favourite pieces of legislation of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition when he was prime minister. I should like to quote from this statute:

It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely,-
I am not going to refer to all of them, but I should like to refer to two that are applicable to this situation. Paragraph (b) reads as follows:
(b) The right of the individual to equality before the law and the protection of the law;
Paragraph (e) reads as follows:
(e) Freedom of assembly and association;
Now, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me it is obvious that there has been flagrant and open violation of these laws. What is more, Mr. Chairman, there is an international law to which Canada has subscribed and which also guarantees protection of our citizens.
I refer, for example, to article 23 of the United Nations charter which reads as follows:
Everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work, and to protection against unemployment.
Article 20 reads:
Everyone has the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and association.
The next sentence reads:
No one may be compelled to belong to an association.
I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that all of this lawlessness that has taken place under that tyrant, and the organization that he heads, has been a violation of these laws, international laws and national laws, to which the Canadian government is committed. If there is a problem as to whether it is up to the provinces to enforce these laws, then we must recognize that new laws must be written and, furthermore, that perhaps there needs to be a redefinition of responsibility. Unless and until the government is prepared to enforce the laws that protect citizens against intimidation, no matter what provisions are written into this trusteeship legislation it will fail to remove the tyranny and lawlessness from the waterfront and on the great lakes.

Maritime Transportation Unions
In the early spring of 1949 representatives of the shipping companies and prominent trade union officials requested Mr. Harry Lundeberg of the United States, international president of the S.I.U., to provide a leader for the S.I.U. in Canada. They went to the United States for a leader, and here is the second reason for these difficulties. Mr. Justice Norris' report clearly outlines Mr. Banks' history in Canada since his arrival.
The final destruction of the independent Canadian seamen's union was as a result of action by the Canada labour relations board in 1959 which revoked the union's certification with one company because, as the board stated, "being communist dominated it was no longer a trade union". This is where the board got on very sticky ground.
Strangely enough, in 1959 the Canada labour relations board, the same board, rejected the claim that communist affiliation or domination was a sound reason for decertification of an otherwise properly operated union. The fact of the matter is that the government, the companies and the union leaders concerned wished to get rid of the C.S.U. and replace it with the seafarers' international union, and the result of their success can be found in the pages of Mr. Justice Norris' report.
First of all, they wished to obey the wishes of the S.I.U. to give these seamen to the United States union's jurisdiction, and second, some of them used the pretext that some of the leadership were communists. Let me say without any hesitation that any man in public life whose chief stock in trade is anti-communism, and with little else behind it, will support an3r form of dictatorship when he gets in a corner.
As I have said, the result of their success can be found in the pages of Mr. Justice Norris' report and also in the disappearance of Canadian ships from the high seas. There is no doubt a relationship between these two incidents.
Before proceeding further I wish to give full credit to the officers and members of two exceptions, must share some responsibility for developing the hysteria and political smokescreen that surrounded the activities of Mr. Banks in Canada. The only daily paper I know of that opposed Banks irregular importation was the Victoria Colonist, and the only other papers I know of that editorially attacked Banks for his day to day activities were the Globe and Mail and the Toronto Telegram. These last two were promptly sued for libel, and Banks was able to collect $3,000 damages as a result of

a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada because his so-called good character had been somewhat tarnished.
All this was going on while the government smiled benignly and the police stood by inactive. At one period I had 25 seamen, most of them fellows who had served during the second world war in the Canadian merchant fleet and the Royal Canadian Navy, in my office to protest against the frightening state of affairs which existed, but they could not get a hearing in those days. One could hardly get a hearing in this house, and certainly the press did nothing to inform the public of this unfortunate state of affairs. At that time the newspapers in general lauded Mr. Banks' version of democracy at work, and as 1 say, so far as I can remember there were only these few papers which took a stand.
Before proceeding 1 want to deal with an interesting editorial entitled "Newshawks Goofed on Banks Scandal" which appeared in the July 18 issue of the Northern Daily News published in Kirkland Lake, Ontario.

Mr. Justice Norris' stern indictment of the seafarers' international union regime on the great lakes marks a long overdue judgment.
In fact it has been overdue since the day S.I.U. boss Hal Banks first stepped across the border with his thugs to take over control of jobs on Canadian ships.
At this point one can be permitted a little sardonic laughter at the virtuous tone being adopted by Canadian authorities and newspapers as they hasten to step in line behind the Norris report of skullduggery on the lakes.
Because authorities, police and particularly the country's newspapers, stood solidly behind the importation of Banks to this country and hurrahed almost to a man while his goon squads beat up legitimate Canadian seamen and forced them off the nation's ships-
So what's the story now?
Excluding great lakes vessels, instead of 100 ships there were at last count, two deep sea freighters under Canadian registry. The trained seamen are long since dispersed and forgotten, including the ones who risked death to transport supplies and fuel across the wartime Atlantic.
Can't blame Banks for all this, but it's a coincidence.
Before proceeding further I wish to give full credit to the officers and members of the Canadian brotherhood of railway transport and general workers and the national association of marine engineers, and of other unions, as a valiant band of trade unionists fighting under most difficult circumstances to restore democracy in the operation of maritime unions. These men deserve a great deal of credit. They did not get much encouragement to start with, and we all owe them a debt of gratitude. Because of their

courage and persistence they were mainly responsible for the Norris inquiry, with its shocking revelations of the rotten fruits that have ripened from the seeds that were sown in 1949. There is where the trouble started. Without a doubt, Mr. Chairman, there is a growing demand among trade unionists for more autonomy and control of their own affairs. I can tell that from mixing up with trade unionists. When I want to find out what labour is thinking, I meet with the rank and file. I am only a simple old backwoodsman, but I go around and speak to these people; I address them at their meetings. They always receive me cordially, especially when I tell them that I have never enjoyed the net income of a village plumber, or something of that sort. Therefore they realize we have a great deal in common. These are the people I talk to. I talked to the unions in my constituency about this matter when I went home. I have addressed them about this. I addressed them, in fact, with one Scottish labour M.P. just before I came to Ottawa. He was actually horrified at the suggestion of a trusteeship over Canadian trade unions. But then they have a different situation over there; Britain is a unitary state and they have not experienced these international problems, and gangsterism. Anyway, Mr. Chairman, without a doubt there is a growing demand among Canadian trade unionists for more autonomy and control of their own affairs. While promoting the spirit of fraternity with all democratic labour organizations, they wish to be master in their own house.
1 want to illustrate this development, and I rejoice in it. I have had a hand in it. In my constituency the workers in the Castlegar pulp mill became members of the paper workers union something over three years ago. They decided at the end of the contract, at the end of two years, that they were not getting satisfactory service, so they had a vote. With the exception of three or four employees, some hundreds of men voted to join the Canadian section of the international union of pulp and sulphite workers. What was the result of that? They were acceptable to the C.L.C. at that time. The international president of the pulp and sulphite workers union was compelled by Mr. George Meany to return a charter issued to the workers in the Celgar Corporation which, as I said before, had been accepted by the C.L.C. Mr. Meany ordered that the papermakers had jurisdiction over this plant and said that this matter had been decided in Washington. As a result today, I am proud to say, they have local No. 1 of a
Maritime Transportation Unions Canadian pulp and sulphite union and three or four other pulp mills in British Columbia have followed their example.
In the very near future they are about to form the national union of Canadian pulp and sulphite workers. I give that as an illustration of this outcropping of a desire for more autonomy. Mind you, they want fraternity, co-operation and things of that sort. This sort of action on the part of leaders in the United States only promotes and develops the desire for autonomy.
I wish to bring to the committee's attention another document which I have here in my hand. It is an agreement drafted, but not signed as yet, between the B.C. hydro authority and an organization known as the Columbia Hydro Contractors Limited. This draft agreement is intended to cover all the workers who will be employed in the erection of dams, the construction of generating facilities and transmission facilities on the Columbia river, should that development go ahead. This draft agreement is not the result of a consultation with Canadian citizens. This agreement, covering years of work that may be undertaken by Canadian workers, was drafted as the result of a meeting between the officials of the British Columbia hydro authority and Mr. Keenan, an A.F. of L. official of the building trades section in Washington. You have no idea what a storm this is creating among some of our Canadian trade unionists. This draft agreement establishes conditions under which Canadian workers will obtain employment on government projects on the Columbia before a man is ever hired on the job or work is commenced.

I fully appreciate the deep concern of all hon. members of this house in their efforts to find a solution of this unfortunate and unusual situation. However, I must say that I cannot agree with the principle of this resolution for several reasons. I have given this a lot of thought. I am a chap who is inclined to listen to what other people say. I was brought up in a very democratic home where there was a tremendous respect for the rights of the individual. My old father used to defend the revolutionaries, the members of the I.W.W., when they came to speak in our district. Men came whom people wanted to toss in the lake, and that sort of thing. On one occasion a meeting was to be addressed by a Mr. Stirling. He was going to speak on the coming social revolution. He was a member of the legislature later. The meeting was to be held in a small village. The board of trade arranged for a group of first world war veterans in 1919 to go down to the boat to throw him into the lake. He could have gone on, but if he got off he was to be thrown into the lake. My father rushed down to the wharf. He went down there with his whiskers drooping down, like the characters you see on the stage on occasion. He went up to these men and broke up the gathering. He said, "This country has been established on British democratic principles and under British democratic institutions, and this man has the right to talk all the bloody rot he wishes provided he is not rude to Her Majesty and does not abuse the law of the land".
I have tried to live in that way ever since. That is why I get into trouble at times. I go to meetings that I should not go to and I

address other forbidden meetings. I do this in the Hyde park tradition which gives every man an opportunity to say what he thinks as long as he remains within the law. This background and belief causes me to give this legislation a great deal of thought. I respect the views of those who do not agree with me. I am sure there is no one who is happy about this situation. But I cannot agree with the principle of this resolution which proposes to establish a trusteeship over the unions for five years without there being any mention of the companies concerned. I agree with what our leader had to say about that. Why establish a trusteeship over the unions without bringing the companies, which have been guilty in many respects under the same jurisdiction and control? I know it is possible, since shipping comes under the jurisdiction of the national government, for the government to draft legislation which would provide for some supervision over these steamship companies.
Second, I am of the opinion that the legislation contemplated will provoke and increase international incidents both at government level and at international union level. I was interested in the speech made by the hon. member for Halifax. I wish to congratulate him; I thought he made an excellent contribution to this debate. He had some doubts about the wisdom of the course we are following. He said the legislation might fail. I am of the opinion that it will bring about serious complications on the international scene.
My third reason for objecting to this legislation is that a large section of the rank and file of the organized labour movement in Canada is opposed to it. I do think the truth should have been given to these people far earlier; there should have been an opportunity for a further discussion on this whole situation. Fourth, I oppose this measure on the ground that it completely overlooks and underestimates the democratic strength and understanding of the Canadian labour movement and its ability to mobilize the support of the rank and file. I think this is a great opportunity for labour to act, first, in defence of Canadian sovereign rights, second, in the defence of democratic principles and institutions and, third, in the development of the complete control of Canadian unions by Canadians for Canadians, operated in the Canadian way.
I have given this subject some thought. It is not easy for me to differ from my colleagues, because I am a sensitive soul. But I do urge the government, as did the leader of our party, to give consideration to the reduction of the period of trusteeship and to incorporate in this legislation provision for

the supervision of the companies directly concerned. With this brief outline of my views, I will conclude. It is my intention to outline some alternative proposals on the second reading of the bill.
