Mr. Chairman, I do not want to take much of the time of the committee to discuss the resolution before us. However, I am interested in it for two reasons: first because I am a member of the house, and second, because I had the opportunity for several years of my life to hold positions in labour movements, that is I was president of labour locals for a number of years. So I am well aware of the justification for labour unions.
I know that labour unions were born because of a great need, the need for workers to protect themselves against employers who went too far and were unfair to them in many ways. Hence it was employers who compelled the workers to unite in order to obtain together what they could not obtain separately. That was a very good reason to set up unions.
It was also the best means for workers to defend themselves, but on one condition: once established, those unions should be free, have their autonomy and the most complete freedom for workers to use their rights and establish their own rules, provided of course the rules are in accordance with the law of the land.
That is why I have always been and still am in favour of a very great freedom for unions.
Obviously, it is a privilege of democracies that people be their own rulers, that workers and professional people control their own business, and together try to find the best ways to achieve the highest possible degree of welfare.
But liberty and freedom do not mean licence. There are limits to these words. If I understand them correctly, they mean the right to choose as long as the use of a right does not interfere with the liberty of others. That is exactly what is going on now in the seamen's unions whose actions, with their possible disastrous effects we are now discussing. What I mean is that those people, at a certain time, acted somewhat like employers did in the past.
Workers have been forced to unite against employers because of injustice committed by the latter, but this freedom to unite does not now give workers the right to be unjust toward the rest of society outside their unions.
That is why I am not far from approving the measure introduced now by the government, precisely because I am against the abuse of freedom which has been committed, if I
Maritime Transportation Unions may say so, in such a glaring way by the presidents of the seamen's unions, especially the S.I.U.
The situation which we have to deplore at the present time has not developed overnight, but gradually, due to several causes, and I think one of them rests on the fact that we have for too long been allowing our unions to Americanize.
I realize that at the beginning, it was quite difficult for Canadian unions to organize and to administer themselves, but now that we have become an adult nation, I think it is high time that workers, if they want to be the masters of the situation in their own country and not be forced to obey orders coming from outside the country, should unite and realize that our unions must not be international unions any more, but Canadian unions. And that is only one reason among thousands of others.
That we are right in our contention, and we deplore it at the present time, is quite obvious in the seafarers' unions. And it is not a unique case in Canada.
There are other fields where the same situation is brewing. The government should not wait until it is too late before acting, otherwise we shall be faced with the same situation in railway unions.
There again, those unions are under American control.
The same thing exists in the field of entertainment. I should like to read part of a letter from one of my constituents dealing precisely with this matter:
I am not too familiar with labour matters, but there is a field that I know comparatively well, that is show business, more particularly variety entertainment. I can assure you, sir, that in the last ten years or so, French-Canadian artists had to pay over one quarter million dollars, that is about $25,000 a year, to a foreign organization called "The American Guild of Variety Artists" (AGVA), which has its headquarters in New York and a branch in Montreal.

As I was saying, Mr. Chairman, when I pointed out that it was six o'clock, in the present case, that of the S.I.U. the government is compelled to act on account of the abuses disclosed by the Norris investigation.
Hal Banks came to Canada for the sole purpose, in co-operation with some shipping companies, of violating and breaking existent collective agreements as well as using any available means to destroy other unions and thus consolidate his own position.
We also know that there were some irregularities in connection with hiring, pension

funds, etc. The Norris report clearly indicates that the situation will not be settled on the great lakes as long as Banks remains at the head of the S.I.U.
It is with reluctance that we must resort to legislation. But, all the same, this legislation is a little better than the lawlessness prevailing at present.
I hope that the minister will give us an idea of the people he intends to appoint to this board. He shall have to act very carefully, because one of its members will necessarily have to mix with workers in order to find the best way of helping them to regain control of their union.
If the trusteeship is administered properly, it will ensure the future of the labour movement, but if the reverse happens because of bad appointments, the future of the S.I.U. will remain very doubtful.
One has only to read the Norris report about the strife on the great lakes to realize that labour legislation is in an alarming situation.
I know that all those conflicts between unions should open our eyes wider and lead us to ask ourselves if the time has not come for the government to set up a commission of inquiry on union activities in Canada and especially those of American unions in our country. That does not mean that unions are not good, but some union leaders should be put in their place.
Such a commission would enable the government and especially the Department of Labour to tackle the job of providing the labour movement with a federal code, a code which should be prepared with the co-operation of the unions, the provinces and representatives of industry, so that we may not be faced again with a situation such as the one which forced the government to put the S.I.U. under trusteeship.
I know that when we come to problems involving the workers and union activities in particular, we must take all the necessary precautions to avoid disputes between governments and trade unions. But if, for a number of years, the government had not accepted the abuses of some union leaders and if it had taken a stand, with positive action defining clearly its role towards the unions, we would not have today to take compulsory measures against union members. We have no choice. We must take the necessary means to ensure peace and security on the great lakes.
However, a government trusteeship has some good points: first, it will be useful to get rid of Banks and his gang; then it will promote a closer watch on collective bargaining, thereby ensuring that the union members regain control over their unions.
Maritime Transportation Unions
I support this legislation because it will allow Canadians to regain control of their business; but this does not mean that by passing that legislation all problems will be solved.
I hope nevertheless that all this will be a lesson to the government and, as I said earlier, the setting up of a commission of inquiry on union activities in Canada and especially those of American unions in our country would permit us to get a labour code in order to give Canadian workers the security and justice to which they are entitled.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is most unfortunate that Canada has reached the state where it is going to have to impose compulsory trusteeship on a number of unions. I believe this is not only a reflection on the Canada labour relations board and the other agencies set up to project the workers and to allow them free association in the great union movement but there has also been a complete failure of the legal procedures available to the average citizen to correct things that have nothing whatsoever to do with unionism. I think this is a very sad state of affairs, particularly when today we hear compulsory arbitration and trusteeship being referred to by some members and being given somewhat the same kind of support.
There is no need to go into the history of Banks. I called him a gangster many years ago in this house. I know he has a number of henchmen who are completely dependant upon him and who have made it possible for him to maintain his position. I do not know, and I am not even going to hazard a guess, whether a trusteeship will correct this situation or will not, but I think it is generally understood that throughout the world the free trade union movement is destroyed initially by the implementation of trusteeship and compulsory abitration. I mention them both because it would appear that if any difficulty should arise in the labour movement in the near future one or the other is going to be recommended by every reactionary employer in the country. I hasten to add that I do not think this will happen with the present Minister of Labour, nor would it have with the previous minister of labour. I think these two gentlemen have done a very good job in administering the operation of the acts which are their responsibility. I think it is very foolish for the Canadian public to be given the impression that they did not do all that was within their power to solve the problem as they saw it. I feel that this is all they have to do, and that they have done it.

Maritime Transportation Unions
There are improvements that must be made in our laws in order to make the settlement of many of these problems easier. This may mean that we shall have to take a look at some of the things that have caused this matter to reach the stage it has. One of these things is the hiring hall, Mr. Chairman. If you were to eliminate the hiring hall you would probably eliminate a great many of the problems facing this particular union, as well as other unions that are in almost the same category.
This afternoon the house was made aware of the fact that there is a union in the process of negotiating a contract in the Columbia river area in connection with the building of a dam that we have not considered yet.
I do not believe anyone is in a position of knowing who the principals are going to be in connection with that construction. I believe, therefore, this whole problem is being repeated there and also must be faced. I do not believe the way to face it is the establishment of a trusteeship, because this will be a crutch on which the people in the labour movement, management and many others will lean, especially if we make it a popular and acceptable thing. Many totalitarian countries throughout the world have used similar methods to destroy the free trade union movement. I think most rank and file trade union members are violently opposed to trusteeship in any form. Certainly, they must be opposed to legislative trusteeship because, for many of them, this eliminates any democratic rights they may have.
Now, Mr. Chairman, what was the real reason for the recommendation of Mr. Justice Norris to take over five unions rather than one? I ask this question. Would it not have been better if this one union were to be taken over? This would still allow the workers along the seaway and the great lakes to join another union of their choice in that field. Nothing wrong was found in connection with these unions, and yet they have been asked to go into trusteeship voluntarily, along with the union in which we are trying to correct the problem. I ask, is this being fair to the membership of these unions? Most of them have had no opportunity of deciding for themselves whether or not they want to accept voluntary trusteeship. Is this the price the labour movement in general is going to have to pay for the next four or five years to get peace on the great lakes? Has justice reached the stage where Banks cannot be removed in any other way than the application of a trusteeship?
I have had something to do with unions in the past, and have had something to do with communist dominated unions. We found that

in those unions you had two or three communists, or a half dozen at the outside, per 100 members, and yet they were able, in many cases, to dominate the union. When the other 95 out of 100 members decided to stand on their two feet and fight back, then usually what we are trying to accomplish here was accomplished by the working people themselves. It is for this reason I say the labour relations act itself must be overhauled. Obviously, this type of machinery is not available to the workers on the great lakes, and particularly those who have been made captives by the S.I.U. We are all aware of the abuses that have been made of certain procedures, such as the hiring halls, "do not ship" lists, the accumulation of vast sums of money through the operation of pension plans, and vacations with pay plans, which have been improperly administered. I wonder if there are not many other forms of assistance that could be given in this field without the imposition of trusteeship?
Now, Mr. Chairman, we have heard of the fact that the S.I.U. is a bad union. In my opinion, a bad union really does not exist because it has bad leadership alone. It is bad because it has bad leadership in conjunction with bad management. Unless a deal could have been worked out between Mr. Banks and the personnel agents of Canada Steamship Lines, no deal would have been made. Because these two people were evil in character, the deal they made was bad. However, I believe it is obvious to everyone that there was another deal made by a union on the great lakes in which the company cooperated with the union in making this type of arrangement, but it was not bad because of the people that were involved. I suggest that if we had the legal machinery, we would have been able to ask for a report from Mr. Robinette and Mr. Martineau, which would have indicated in all probability a course of action for the solution of this problem by due process of law.
Many people have spoken on this subject. There have been some good speakers from all parts of the house. However, I do not believe I stand alone in opposing trusteeship. I believe most people who have had anything to do with unions know that trusteeship is highly undesirable if it is put into effect in any way, shape or form, but probably the worst form is through the introduction of legislation. Trusteeship by government takes away the rights of the workers. Often a union has to be put under trusteeship because of the inability of the membership to look after their affairs, but when somebody else does this the situation becomes even worse. Has the committee really considered what this

trusteeship is going to accomplish? Have they really considered what the results of this are going to be? Anyone supporting this legislation who thinks it is going to be an immediate success should really consider all the implications.
I have no objection to the Canadian Labour Congress going to some of the officials of the United States government and requesting assistance, because certainly the United States government has come up against this problem that we are facing. The United States government has tried everything possible to dispose of Mr. Hoffa, but every time they do something to him they make him that much stronger. I wonder if we have really considered this matter? I presume the trusteeship legislation will go through because there appears to be no alternative. I am not in a position, Mr. Chairman, to offer any alternative. However, I believe the committee would be well advised to seriously consider the possibility of an alternative. I would think that the house would have been very wise to call the industrial relations committee of this house together to try to find some solution. Other countries have found solutions for this type of problem. I believe many of the members have failed to look towards tomorrow to see what the results of this action are going to be.
I am not saying that a government trusteeship imposed on unions will mean the repeal of the Rush-Bagot treaty, but I am just asking the committee to remember what happened when a Canadian ship was sent down into Chicago to ascertain what the climate would be. That ship has now limped back into Canadian territory and another one has been dispatched in its stead. I only hope we do not have to send down a front line frigate to protect the second ship. It may be a good experiment, but I do not see why this shipping company should keep a ship at Chicago when there are many cargoes to be obtained in other areas. This will be in the history of Canadian shipping when the government sets up a marine corps.
Have hon. members really thought about it? I know the labour movement in the United States is very much opposed to what is happening here as is, in the main, the Canadian labour movement. If the two movements are as strongly opposed to it as they appear to be, then this is not going to be an end to the strike on the great lakes. It will only be the beginning.
We should consider the problem fully, because the international free trade union movement stretches across the world, and we have to consider the possibility of a boycott when we endeavour to get rid of five or six people by means of trusteeship. We may even 28902-5-218
Maritime Transportation Unions have to apply martial law in order to get rid of them; but no matter what the circumstances, we may have to face the problem of delay to Canadian ships operated by government imposed trusteeship.
Have we really thought of all the alternatives? I am not suggesting I know them all, but I do know this is not a solution that is acceptable to many trade unionists throughout Canada. Indeed it is not generally acceptable to trade unionists throughout the world. Although the minister is to be congratulated on all the avenues he has explored so far, I do believe trusteeship is not the answer.
We will get the Canadian trade union movement into a very difficult predicament by proposing legislative trusteeship. I am not familiar with the full situation in Montreal today regarding the longshoremen's strike, but the union involved is a responsible one. It has gone through due process of law. It has asked the federal government for mediation, and this has been provided in the person of a judge. However, I am shocked to see that already hon. members have stood up in this house and talked about compulsory arbitration for this union because it is causing some discomfort in parts of Canada. This is true, and looking at the over-all picture it may have many ramifications; but hon. members should consider the position of the longshoremen who have negotiated through the normal channels of law, who have asked for mediation, and who now find that the general public and many members of parliament are crying for their scalps before they, the workers, have concluded the mediation process.
It would be less than reasonable if the longshoremen did not pick a time to negotiate when the shipping season was at its height. I see nothing wrong in what has happened to date in that situation, but because of gangsterism and the low character of many of those in high places in the S.I.U., the general public is inclined to lump many labour problems into the one basket.
I am not prepared to support compulsory trusteeship. I would certainly be the first to admit something has to be done about this particular problem. Its existence has been known for several years, and for a long time we have been saying Hal Banks was a gangster and should be deported or eliminated from the Canadian labour movement. We should ask ourselves why, through due process of law, in a democratic country and in a democratic manner in the operations of a democratic trade union movement we have not been able, in a judicial manner, to clean up this unholy mess which has brought us to the sad state of affairs we face tonight.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in taking part in this discussion tonight, I am most conscious of the difficulties and problems parliament is facing at the present time in connection with the establishment of a trusteeship for the maritime unions on the great lakes.
Since I am a worker myself and since I have contributed to the establishment of a union, some may think that in contributing to this debate I may be biased; but, Mr. Chairman, we are undertaking today the consideration of a resolution which, in my opinion, has no precedent in the labour history of Canada.
This proposal of the government to establish a trusteeship over the various maritime and stevedores unions on the great lakes and along the St. Lawrence raises many points of principle which we should study with the utmost care.
This legislation for the establishment of a trusteeship is, I am sure, a precedent and that is why we must try to find as clearly as possible the reasons why the government was led to introduce this measure so that, in future years, we may not have to rely on the government or any trusteeship legislation to settle problems which should be settled within the ranks of the labour unions.
This decision results from the unions helplessness in solving a serious problem in the administration of the union concerned as shown by the royal commission appointed in July 1962.
This investigation proved beyond any reasonable doubt that the allegations of the Canadian Labour Congress to the effect that terror and gangsterism have ruled over these unions, among which the seafarers' union, and that the government had therefore an obligation to intervene, first to safeguard the economic interests of Canada and its good name abroad. Second-and this is not the least important reason-to preserve also the rights of the workers and to free them from a reign of terror which kept them in an atmosphere of continuous fear, while their dues were put to dishonest use.
I think the situation we are now facing shows clearly the degree of vigilance the workers must exercise in watching over their interest so they will not be tricked.
Having been exploited for a long time by heartless employers and enterprises, they united and had to fight relentlessly, and it is only after tremendous sacrifices that they were recognized and respected. But nowadays, they have to face other enemies who have infiltrated their ranks so as to take advantage

of the structures and the strength they built and use them for their own illegitimate purposes.
It will be said that loss of control over their union by members is due to the fact that those unions have become too big, too powerful, too complex in their administration and that there, as elsewhere, centralization has prevented the members from retaining contact with their leaders and the management.
I admit that this is one of the causes of the troubles we are now going through. But why do we need those powerful and centralized unions if not to fight against large industrial trusts?
A few decades ago, we had small employers but the situation has changed and, nowadays, we have colossal industrial empires grouping the best administrative brains, assisted by almost every banking and financial system in this country, and even outside.
Mr. Chairman, giants must be opposed by giants and so the conflict resulting from their confrontation inevitably jeopardizes the very basis of our economy and the society in which we live.
Yesterday, I heard the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) suggest that the government refer to a parliamentary committee the problem of amending the country's labour legislation which allowed a situation like that of the great lakes seafarers to develop. I wholeheartedly support this proposal, but I would add that it is just as urgent to review also the legislation providing for the incorporation of companies and the setting up of industrial empires and trusts, in order to eliminate the serious abuses it allows.
Let us consider the part played by the Canada Steamship Lines as mentioned by Mr. Justice Norris in his report.
If we are permitted to judge Mr. Hal Banks severely, I think we must come to the conclusion that those who co-operated with him in that company must also be judged.
They claim that they were forced to act that way, but I am not so sure. If that is the case, they had means available to make the situation known and to ask that an investigation be made.
And what about the part played by the government in this matter? Is it not the government that amended the citizenship and immigration legislation, especially to allow the permanent admission of Hal Banks to Canada?
What about Mr. Jodoin, president of the C.L.C., who strongly endorsed the application of Mr. Banks? However, he admitted having made a mistake, and since he too is a giant in a certain sense, he rightly said that he makes enormous mistakes.

What part was played by American interests in this matter?
The present situation shows, more than ever, the urgent need for all our country's organizations to become autonomous.
Dominated by American unions, dominated by American industries, dominated by American policies, dominated by American defence, the situation is almost hopeless.
And those who listened to the news tonight, heard that the American secretary of labour, as well as president Meany, today declared themselves violently opposed to the setting up of the present trusteeship by the Canadian government. They especially blamed the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, Mr. Jodoin, and accused him of being the first responsible for this legislation which will soon be put into effect.
Mr. Chairman, I think that we have here further convincing evidence of American interference in a field which belongs to us alone. And I urge the government to reply and request the Americans to stay in their own field, because if we are faced today with that problem, it originated with them. Indeed, if they had opposed in time the lawlessness which prevailed in some American labour organizations, that gangsterism would not have been imported into Canada.
Mr. Chairman, the government intends to impose upon the unions concerned a trusteeship of no longer than five years. I hope it will not take that long to settle the problem.
Three people will be entrusted with the delicate and serious task. I am happy to see that four or five of the unions in question have already accepted the trusteeship. That undoubtedly proves that the legislation under consideration has already been endorsed by those who are mainly concerned and we must proceed not only with haste but with extreme care.
Yesterday, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) made a statement which I found rather strange, coming as it did from the leader of a party which advocates strong government control over our national economy.
In fact, as reported on page 3380 of the English version of Hansard for October 9, 1963, he said:
Naturally public trusteeship is unpalatable.
Mr. Chairman, these words sound wrong coming from the leader of the New Democratic party. The same words were repeated this afternoon, this time by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), who opposed rather strongly, while making important reserves, the establishment of this trusteeship. He stated that he would accept it as a makeshift.

Mr. Chairman, circumstances may, at a given time, force or justify the government to take action concerning a labour movement. In such a case, I believe we ought to accept that measure on a temporary basis.
Now, if the followers of a certain socialistic philosophy claim that the government has the power, the greatest capacity, the only authority and competency to administer the economy and the industry of this country, they should, I believe, also recognize to that government the right to put some order into the affairs of certain labour unions, if the members have lost control.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that we ought to call the attention of the general public to this point, so as not to stir up the workers who could see in such a measure some kind of infringement on their liberty. In fact, should anyone conclude that the enactment of this legislation is tantamount to a loss of freedom, then I believe that freedom no longer exists.
When there is disorder, dishonesty, and no longer any possibility for an organization to amend itself, then in my opinion, it is our duty not to criticize the government but to second it, to make to that government suggestions concerning the legislation presently introduced.
The government was very reluctant to take such a step and to some extent I believe it was right, since this state of affairs is altogether unusual. We all hope that one of the results of such trusteeship-and I particularly stress this point-will be to give our unions a true Canadian make-up so that they may be administered by Canadians.
Mr. Chairman, there is also the fact that the contributions of our Canadian workers are being exported to a foreign country through certain labour unions. If we are faced with those problems, it is not only the workers who are to blame; we should also try to find the origin and the cause of those problems.
The powerful Canadian unions, which are now controlled by Americans, came to Canada from the United States at the time when American industries first became established in our country. I think that this was done in order to interfere with a policy followed at a certain time by some American companies which, by setting up branches in various countries, tried to prevent the development of labour unions.
In this connection, I remember a case in particular. If my memory is correct, it concerns the Singer company which manufactures sewing machines and which in order to check the development of the labour movement and deny its right and fair demands has built plants throughout the world, plants

Maritime Transportation Unions which it used to rotate its production from one country to another. Thus, as soon as unions became strong enough in a country, by rotating its production, the company has been in a position to check the labour movement.
Nevertheless, it seems that Providence has avenged the workers since that company by its dealings has forgotten its original purpose and has since been outstripped by its competitors.
Canadian workers are powerful because we have strong industries.
If, by means of a trusteeship, we want to eliminate some serious faults that we find in the labour unions in Canada, we as well as the government itself will probably have to see to it that American companies become themselves Canadian companies, so that the government does not have to suffer the same indignity its ministers suffered recently when they had to deal with some American officials. In fact, five ministers of the Canadian government, supposedly independent and sovereign, had to meet some American officials and ask them permission to increase the production of automotive parts in Canada; and what did they get? A firm refusal, a definite no.

Mr. Chairman, that fully illustrates the seriousness of the problem with which we are faced now. It does not concern only workers' unions; it has become a general cancer which affects our industry and the whole of our economy.
I feel that the present legislation may be a partial solution. I hope it will open the eyes of the parties concerned and that the latter will not wait until the public authorities are forced to impose solutions before they take action.
American owners of industries situated in Canada will have to realize that they are working against our democratic regime by their present behavior. Canada cannot keep on being a satellite of the United States and all of us must stress this fact.
It is quite out of the question for us to quarrel with the Americans in this connection. But I think that if they respect the autonomy of some South American, Caribbean, African and European nations, they should first of all respect the autonomy of their main ally and next door neighbour, Canada.
I believe that if Canada and the United States get together to iron out those problems which are not only Canadian problems but international problems, we can, not under

any coercion, but in a great spirit of justice, resolve the difficulties facing the nation at the present time.
I should also like to emphasize that the French fact is practically ignored by American unions in Canada. I wish to point out that particular aspect in order to show that the problem is very complex. I trust that when control over Canadian unions reverts to Canada now that the English speaking Canadians increasingly realize the advantages of recognizing both cultures in Canada, our Canadian unions, from Vancouver to Halifax, in their negotiations and in their relations with the French Canadian group, will manage to display comprehension and especially justice for that group. This, Mr. Chairman, is not a plea for sympathy but simply an appeal to reason and to common sense.
I also wish to call the attention of the house to another problem which I think is closely related to the one now under consideration, that is the strike which has been going on for several days in seaports along the St. Lawrence seaway in the province of Quebec. This is of particular concern to us in Quebec. I heard that we might have to impose compulsory arbitration. That would amount to an act of despair.
I am of the opinion, Mr. Chairman, that if we were to review all legislation concerning unions and collective bargaining, we would find that to be the source of the problems facing the government in its relations with labour.
It is rather important to note that, each year, in the province of Quebec alone, thousands of collective agreements are signed for which workers did not have to go on strike. To my mind, that shows that workers recognize they have more to gain by negotiating objectively and by respecting the rights and privileges of each and every one than by going on strike indiscriminately. It is also an indication, Mr. Chairman, that legislation now in force in the province of Quebec is better suited than the one now to be found in the federal statutes to solve that problem.

I was speaking about the happy unanimity of the house in connection with this resolution, and I hope that the accident of two members rising at the same time has been forgiven. However, there has been a certain blindness arising from this unanimity, I suggest, and perhaps the committee, as the hon. member for Timiskaming suggested, has not looked carefully enough into the future consequences of this trusteeship. I say that for this reason. The Minister of Labour has exercised, through his versatility and courage, every virtue he could be expected to exercise in this role. He has explored every opportunity. He has probed the basis of a possible private trusteeship. He has tried to negotiate with every possible party to the dispute, and only as a last alternative is he presenting to the house legislation to create a public trusteeship which, repugnant though it may be, has met with the support of every party and every group in this house. So we have a resolution with public opinion behind it. The committee is unanimously behind it, and in the days which follow I think the minister will be entitled to call on the support of the house to implement this trusteeship if it runs into heavy weather, as I believe it is bound to do.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, two reasons why the public trusteeship will encounter difficult times. The first is that a public trusteeship cannot work unless it has the support of the members of the union or unions over which the trusteeship is imposed. I think no better example of that can be cited than the history of the monitorship over the teamsters union in the United States where, in terms of the ultimate vote, Mr. Hoffa retained the support, and the overwhelming support of the union. No matter how the vote was garnered he retained the ultimate support of the union, and against that support of the union the monitorship appointed by the courts was

Maritime Transportation Unions powerless. In decision after decision they were forced to yield power, control and jurisdiction over the teamsters back again to Mr. Hoffa. I come from Montreal and have had some experience of the waterfront there. Not being as innocent perhaps as some members,
I have met Mr. Banks and dealt with him across the table.

What I want to suggest is that so far as I can gather, and this opinion is shared by many who have experience on the waterfront in Montreal, Mr. Banks still has considerable support among the rank and file of his own union because, whatever else may be said, under his leadership the average worker, the average stevedore, the average seaman, has enjoyed an improved standard of living which has blinded him to the lack of democracy in his own union. Because of the subtle propaganda and the subtle yellow journalism used by Mr. Banks and S.I.U., the average member of that union conceives of a trusteeship as something evil that is to be imposed on him.
I suggest to the house that the remedy of a public trusteeship will be difficult and can be rendered impotent unless the real cancer, Mr. Banks, is operated on. Unless he is removed by legal process from the direction of that union, unless he is removed from the country, the trusteeship cannot be as effective as I am sure every member of the house wants it to be.
The second point I wish to bring to the attention of hon. members is that this public trusteeship, because of the negotiations that have preceded it, is going to prompt a certain tension on the lakes between the American and the Canadian authorities. It already has. The statement tonight by Mr. George Meany will, I am sure, prompt every Canadian union member, every Canadian worker, to wonder whether or not at last he should not have control over his own affairs. If this public trusteeship is the result of anything, it is due primarily to the lack of co-operation of the trade union movement in the United States to help to implement on the Canadian side of the border a private trusteeship such as was sought by the Minister of Labour and those who were negotiating on his behalf. So because of the nature of commerce on the great lakes, which is international, we do have a

problem of tension on the lakes that this public trusteeship will not solve, but may provoke.
I say this to you, Mr. Chairman, because of the difficulties of a trusteeship over the membership and because these men are not yet convinced of the necessity for it, and because a trusteeship is inherently repugnant to the average workingman just as it is repugnant to most of us. In addition, because it is going to breed tension between the United States and Canada, it will be a difficult piece of legislation to implement.
I would call upon all members of the house to support this legislation with the same unanimity tomorrow with which they support it tonight, because I think we are convinced tonight that the trusteeship proposed in this resolution is the only remaining alternative. It is not the best type of solution we would want but it is the only reasonable alternative. Surely, Mr. Chairman, memories will hark back to the reasons that have been advanced by all parties tonight so that, when the trusteeship is at the stage where it must be implemented, the government and the minister will have the same unanimous support from the House of Commons that they have received this evening.

Mr. Chairman, to begin with I indicated when I was putting forward a point of order before that it would be very difficult to be original and I do not suppose I will be. However, the last speaker has given me the opportunity to say that I have at least one thing to say that is original. There is not the unanimous support about which he speaks, and I think that is original enough to take care of his statement about being original.
The government under the sponsorship of the Minister of Labour has brought forward the resolution preceding the legislation for one purpose, to clear up the situation on the lakes. It is designed to bring in a trusteeship which is to be given authority to expel the union bosses, and those members of the union executive who may be closely enough associated with Mr. Banks that they should go with him. To me, Mr. Chairman, this is the long way, this is the expensive way to deal with this matter. I cannot understand why the government has not resorted to deportation, or whatever you want to call it, from this country of Mr. Harold Banks. Recalling what the Secretary of State said this afternoon, namely that it could be done directly, I cannot understand why the government does not have the courage to get rid of Mr. Banks, just as they had the courage to bring him in here to do exactly what he is doing today- fight other unions. He was brought in for

that purpose and he is now being put out of office for the same reason; so why not put him out of the country?
I fully agree with the recommendation of a trusteeship in the Norris commission report. For reasons of my own I cannot refer to the Norris commission report this evening, but if my memory serves me right there is another recommendation on page 311 of that report. Some questions have been asked the Minister of Justice in the house as recently as this afternoon involving one approach which, if followed through, would provide us with the answer, I think, to the trouble brought on us by Mr. Banks. It would not be a matter of deporting him, because I believe what Mr. Justice Norris had to say in that regard.
The deportation of Hal Banks is not going to solve this problem in any way, shape or form. However, if the prosecutions that the Norris commission report also recommends were followed through and if the courts in Quebec and Ontario were to press these matters, it is quite possible that Mr. Banks might wind up where he belongs-behind bars- where he would do nobody any harm.
It is very interesting to me to listen to the speeches from different parts of the house, especially from the far left. This evening one member speaking on behalf of the New Democratic party continually said that that party had referred to Mr. Banks as a gangster. I can stand here and say that I used the word "gangster" with regard to Mr. Banks in the house some years ago and, as I recall, only one member of that party, the hon. member for Kootenay West, consistently spoke against Mr. Banks. I do not recall any others. In fact, when I was condemning Mr. Banks and the type of union he was running I myself was condemned for doing so on many occasions.
I have taken a stand where necessary against union leaders, and this does not apply only to the S.I.U. It strikes me as very strange that some members should get up and complain about something the previous government did not do. I would remind each and every one of them that when the former minister of labour and the former government were called upon by the Canadian Labour Congress, the former government set up the Norris commission. But can you imagine what would have happened if that government had tried to move in and impose a trusteeship at that time upon unions that were having their problems within the Canadian Labour Congress or, if not within the congress, then among themselves? They were trying to settle something among themselves. Can you imagine what repercussions there would have been if any government had
Maritime Transportation Unions stepped in at a time like that and tried to impose any kind of legislation on them?

enforce the law.

Yes, in about 20 minutes. It is a well known fact that when members of this house were criticizing the activities of Mr. Banks a few years ago, none other than Claude Jodoin, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, came to his defence in the courts and said that he would make a valuable citizen. I have reason to believe that today the same Mr. Jodoin would like to back away from the position he has taken. I say this strictly on my own and I could be entirely wrong. However, I have reason to believe that the Canadian Labour Congress regrets this hasty action. I believe that the union men can see far enough ahead, and in this I agree with the last speaker, to realize that ridding the S.I.U. of Mr. Banks is not going to help the situation. I think it will be a case of going from the frying pan into the fire, as has been indicated by the last press release by the United States. We can look forward to a lot of trouble in United States ports.
Now, this whole situation developed, first of all, because two unions could not get along. They fought for the right to represent the seamen on the lakes. Then, from there we step up into another category, and we find that the Canadian Labour Congress cannot reach an agreement with the A.F.L.-C.I.O. Then, we have one more step, Mr. Chairman, and that is the step to government. We find that the Canadian government cannot reach an agreement with the United States government. I believe that the two governments should get together. Everyone in the house has said this is a responsibility of government, and the government should do this or that. I believe it is now the responsibility of both governments to get together and assure one another that if this trusteeship legislation is put into effect, Canadian ships will receive proper service and proper protection while they are in United States ports and vice versa. I believe this is the responsibility of the two governments.
I do not believe there has been a speaker, at least from the opposition parties, who has not said that he feels this is a government responsibility. Many of them have said it was a responsibility of the former government. Nevertheless, it is still the responsibility of this government. They talk about trusteeship. The Canadian people gave them a trusteeship to run this country, and yet the government is now asking some individual citizens to take

Maritime Transportation Unions upon themselves the responsibility of the trusteeship. I say set it up within your own cabinet; show some leadership.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
You can laugh; go ahead and laugh. You laughed this afternoon, but you are not going to laugh me off the floor of this house. I say it is the responsibility of this government to get together with the United States government in order to ensure that Canadian ships will get proper protection and service while in United States ports. Only then is a trusteeship of any kind going to work. I do say to the government that there is no reason this trusteeship cannot be set up within parliament itself, from within the government ranks. This would be the best way for the government to keep an eye on what is happening. If this is not done, questions will be asked in the house from time to time about what the trustees are doing in relation to cleaning up the union, and ministers will be saying, "I expect a report on that in a few days, and I will advise the house later." This will go on for weeks and months. As the leader of the N.D.P. said, the government proposes a five-year term in order to get this union cleaned up. The same hon. member said that this was almost like giving the trustees an absolute dictatorship.
Now, if you cut the period back from five years to two years or even one year, that same description applies. Why does this government feel duty bound to put the responsibility on three private citizens if this legislation goes through? It is the government's responsibility. The first step in connection with that responsibility is on the road to Washington. They are the great friends of the United States. They are the ones who were going to bring this country back to its proper level in international affairs. Let them go down to Washington now and reach an agreement with Mr. Wirtz, if they are duty bound to put in this trusteeship, so that Canadians will receive the proper protection. I think this is properly the first step to take. Before the government imposes any responsibility on others, let them get their own business done.
One thing that surprised me was that everybody talked about a solution. When I was listening to the different speakers and heard everyone say he was against trusteeship but would have to support it, I was surprised no one thought of another solution. This is all nonsense. As long as there are any blameless members of the S.I.U., they should not suffer for the sins of Hal Banks and his executive officers. The last speaker referred to Mr. Banks getting the support of his union. He said, don't you realize how this support is gathered in from all around the country? As

I said a number of years ago, I know the gangsters. I am not standing up in this house to take credit for what somebody else did. Again, I refer to the fact that while we were doing this there were individuals who were clearly criticizing us. At the same time, as I say, Mr. Claude Jodoin of the Canadian Labour Congress was standing up on behalf of Mr. Banks before the immigration committee. Then, too, a former C.C.F. member in this house championed Mr. Banks' cause as legal counsel. This was done by a member of that party which is closely associated with the Canadian Labour Congress.
I have belonged to unions for many years. I have union support. I can get down there and understand the feelings of the union men as well as anybody else in the house. I tell you this, gentlemen, the trouble with our labour unions and labour congresses in this country is that there are too many professional men, and the union membership does not have a chance to voice its opinions. They have, in Mr. Banks, a professional. He is a professional import. There are many other professionals in unions throughout this country. These are the same professionals who, years ago, stood hand in hand with the same Mr. Banks whose scalp they are now after.
Let us return to that solution I mentioned and which I was surprised was not suggested by the N.D.P. They have said they are against the trusteeship, but they have to go along with the government in principle. However, I fully agree with the leader of the N.D.P. when he said that there was another party equally to blame in this affair. What about the steamship lines, the executives of these companies? They are just as responsible for this situation today as the union men. Is the government just going to slap their wrists for being naughty and, at the same time, condemn the unions and the union men who may have been blameless? Why does the government not go after Mr. Banks? You do not have to impose a trusteeship on every man in the country to accomplish that. I refer again to the words of the Secretary of State when he said it could be done directly. Why does the government not go after these steamship companies and slap them around, as I hope they will do with Mr. Banks?
Let me return now to this solution that I was surprised no one mentioned. This is where the N.D.P. surprised me. Apparently this plank is missing from their platform now. I thought they were going to make the suggestion that since we were taking over the unions under trusteeship, they would advocate that the steamship lines should be nationalized along with the unions. This was another way they could once again have got back at

the shipping companies for their part in the fiasco which is taking place today.
When hon. members opposite talk about unanimous support I do not intend at any time to stand here and allow a speaker, especially in another part of the house, to speak for the whole house, particularly when I have no intention of supporting something that is going to be imposed on the labouring man, and something which is being imposed upon him because of a gangster dominated union. I say to the government, deal with the problem directly rather than through this long and expensive route to reach the same end.
I could be wrong, but I am quite sure I heard the Secretary of State say this afternoon that it could be done directly. If so, let the government have the courage to do it. Let the members of the government pack their bags, go down to Washington, and ensure that we get the protection we need.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it was not my intention to take part in this debate, and my intervention at this point will be brief. Although I feel very strongly about some of the things to which I shall refer, I shall keep quite cool. In fact I think that is something we are going to have to do in this field of labour relations, particularly in the labour relations between this country and the United States in the months and years that lie ahead.
I shall not repeat the elements of our position that have been expressed so effectively by the leader of this group, the hon.
28902-5-219
Maritime Transportation Unions member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, and later by the hon. member for Winnipeg North. There is no question but that we stand, as does the trade union movement of this country, against the principle of government trusteeships over free trade unions.
Surely it is clear, however, that what we are faced with now is not the problem of dealing with a free trade union but the problem of dealing with a gangster outfit in a situation where there is no alternative but to bring in the force of law. In so far as, for a limited period of time, a trusteeship is being imposed upon four other unions, which have been declared by Mr. Justice Norris to have a clean bill of health, let it be quite clear that those unions have indicated their willingness to have this trusteeship placed on them, in order that the mess on the great lakes might be cleared up.
However, as has already been said by others of this group, the one feature in this legislation that we feel should be changed- and which we hope will be changed before it goes through all its stages-is the provision for the trusteeship to last for five years.
We feel that this job can, and must be done, in a much shorter period, and it would be far better to have the legislation provide for the trusteeship to last for two years or three years at the most. If the government would like to amend the bill by providing that at the end of that period it could be extended by resolution of both houses of parliament, rather than going through all the stages of the bill again, perhaps that would be appropriate and might be considered. However, apart from making that point, I do not wish to repeat what has been said by those who have already spoken for this group.
Rather, I felt that from this corner of the house something should be said tonight to express our regret at the two statements which have come out of Washington today, the statement of Mr. George Meany, president of the A.F.L.-C.I.O., and the statement of secretary of labour Wirtz. As a matter of fact Mr. Jodoin, president of the Canadian Labour Congress, has already issued a statement in reply to what these two gentlemen have said, and I am in complete agreement with what Mr. Jodoin has said.
So far as Mr. Meany's comments are concerned, I go along with Mr. Jodoin's generosity to Mr. Meany in suggesting that he must not have all the facts in his possession and must not know what is going on in Canada, or he could not possibly come to the defence of Hal Banks and his S.I.U. as though he were defending a free union.
When Mr. Meany complains about the C.L.C. going along with government action to

Maritime Transportation Unions deal with a matter of this kind, it is a bit strange that coincidental with his press release there is a release by secretary of labour Wirtz that suggests there is almost an understanding, if not something stronger, between Mr. Meany and the United States department of labour. I find this inconsistent with the position he has taken with regard to the decision made by the Canadian Labour Congress.
I also agree with Mr. Jodoin in his remarks about what secretary of labour Wirtz has done by way of releasing information about the private negotiations that went on, the negotiations that did not succeed. Surely it is the height of indiscretion for a cabinet minister in another country to reveal afterwards what some of those private negotiations were. In all probability he has not told the whole of the story. In all probability there are other aspects of that story that should be told by the C.L.C.; but when this sort of thing goes on it does no good.
As a trade unionist I object very strongly to the statements made today by Mr. Meany and Mr. Wirtz. I know that the officers of the C.L.C. and the executive council of that congress will deal with their counterparts in the United States through the usual channels, to try to get back to a reasonable understanding of these matters; but I call upon the government of Canada, through its usual channels, to take up with Mr. Wirtz his indiscretion in saying the things he has today. These two gentlemen should not be interfering in this Canadian problem. They should be spoken to, Mr. Meany by the Canadian Labour Congress and Mr. Wirtz by the government of this country.
May I make it clear, Mr. Chairman, that the statements made by Mr. Meany and Mr. Wirtz will not in any way change the views of the members of the executive council of the Canadian Labour Congress who, to my knowledge, have wrestled with this problem over many weeks and many years. In fact, Mr. Chairman, I might note that there are people in this chamber who have been denying they ever met Hal Banks, and there are others who have told of their associations with him. I am one of those who has met Hal Banks. I know the kind of person he is. I met him when I was a vice president and a member of the executive council of the Canadian Labour Congress. I am one member on the floor of this house who has voted against Hal Banks. I was a member of the executive council of the Canadian Labour Congress which, after having him before us, after hearing the evidence, expelled him not only from the Canadian Labour Congress but from the house of free labour in Canada. That was done by an executive council of 21 
members in 1959, and that executive council today is still a body of 21 members. I ask hon. members to realize that of those 21-I am checking in my memory as I go over the names of them; I know them quite well -not more than four, and I think only three, are members of distinctively Canadian unions. The other 17 or 18 are members of international unions; some of them are high ranking officers in those international unions.
If there is anything to the supposed influence of the United States connection, surely it would reflect itself in the attitudes of these members of the executive council of the Canadian Labour Congress. But no. Despite the fact that they are members of international unions; despite the fact that many of them are high ranking officers in international unions, with their international presidents being Americans, they approach this question from the standpoint of Canadian interests, from the standpoint of the interests of free trade unionism in this country. They have taken their stand as to what should be done to clean up this situation. I know them very well. They are not going to be deflected from the stand they have taken; they are not going to change their decision because of the statements that have been issued today from Washington by Mr. Meany and Mr. Wirtz.
I said I wanted to keep cool about this. I feel pretty strongly about it, because what Mr. Meany has done is not in the best traditions of North American international trade unionism. I was at the founding convention of the Canadian Labour Congress in Toronto in 1956. I was a delegate to it from the Winnipeg local of an international union. I remember Mr. Meany being at that convention. I remember his speech to that convention in which he welcomed wholeheartedly the setting up of a Canadian national labour centre that had within its ranks the great majority of the trade unionists of Canada. He asserted that at that point any residual remains of United States control over aspects of the Canadian trade union movement were to be turned over to the new Canadian Labour Congress. There was established at that point something that was an advance over what had existed in previous years, namely a recognition of equality of the two centres, the A.F.L.-C.I.O. in Washington and the Canadian Labour Congress here in Ottawa.
When Mr. Meany made that statement in 1956, in my view he was speaking in the best traditions of North American international trade unionism. In my view this has to exist. We have to get back to it. I stand here tonight, not shouting at Mr. Meany, not complaining, not condemning him, but pleading with him from my place in this Canadian

House of Commons to leave the solution of this problem to the Canadian trade union movement, to the national unions in Canada and to the Canadian sections of the international trade unions in this country, which have worked well through the years, which will continue to work well.
The sort of thing that has now happened must be straightened out. As I see it, it can be done. The Canadian Labour Congress will, I am sure, play its part in straightening this matter out with Mr. Meany. But the Canadian government has also got to straighten out with Mr. Wirtz what he has done in disclosing the partial information he has released today.
I have already said that I am a member of an international union, the international typographical union, and I have been an officer of the Canadian Labour Congress. I was its executive vice president for four years. I know a little bit about the operations of the trade union movement from the viewpoint of its national centre. Those of us who have been at that level know that Canadian trade unionism has a place for, and needs within its ranks, both kinds of unions, some that are distinctively national and some with their international connections. I recognize that it is very popular today, particularly in the light of the kind of things that are happening, to say, "Let us break all these connections and run everything here in this country". Well, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that if our good relations on the North American continent in other fields are to be upheld-in business, commerce, art, culture, industry and all the rest of it-it is not possible for us to live in complete isolation north of the 49th parallel. We must have our relationships of one kind and another. When you are dealing with huge industries like steel or auto and many others I could name, it just does not make sense to say that our workers in Canada must deal with United States employers through their branch plants in Canada in isolation from their fellow workers south of the line. I think there is a place for both kinds of trade unionism in Canada, national and international. This is part and parcel of the constitution of the Canadian Labour Congress. The C.L.C. was set up on that basis. This has produced strains. There is hardly ever a meeting of the executive council of the Canadian Labour Congress, and there is never a convention of that body, that does not have strains with which to contend in these situations. But it was set up on that basis and it is on that basis that in my view it has to be continued. But it will continue and it will succeed in so far as the international unions are concerned only if the international conventions 28902-5-21PJ
Maritime Transportation Unions deal only with matters of policy that are common to the workers in both countries. By the same token, there must be left to the workers in the separate countries complete control of their own affairs.
This is the way the members of the international unions in this country-and please remember that about 65 per cent or 70 per cent of the organized workers in Canada are members of international unions-want it to be, because of the strength it gives to them. But they also know it will work in the long run only, in so far as Canadian affairs are concerned, if these affairs are left to our workers here in Canada. It is on that basis that I am satisfied the executive council of the Canadian Labour Congress made the decision that it made some weeks ago to accept trusteeship as the only alternative. Yet despite the fact that it made the decision some weeks ago, it has wrestled with the proposition; it has tried to find an alternative; it has listened to the suggestions of those who have asked them to consider various alternatives. But they came up with the final decision, in the light of the mess on the lakes, in the light of the gangsterism of Banks, that there is no alternative but to accept this trusteeship, voluntarily accepted by four of the maritime transportation unions but necessarily imposed on the one of which Banks is the head.
Having accepted that, they will give the government their support in seeing that this trusteeship is administered effectively, and they will look, as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George said, for support not only from the government but from all parties in the house, the majority of whom at any rate are in favour of the step that is being taken tonight. So I say that I welcome the idea that there should be more Canadian autonomy over Canadian affairs. This should be true in all aspects of our life, economic, industrial, intellectual, educational, cultural and all the rest. We must have it.

speechtext:
Somebody says military; and defence as well. Yes, add those areas also because they are areas in which we have to live. We cannot separate ourselves completely and our relationship must be maintained. It must be maintained in all of these fields,-but I am speaking particularly of the trade union field. If we are going to have international unions and they are to succeed, there has to be mutual respect on both sides. Claude Jodoin and his fellow officers of the executive council of the Canadian Labour Congress must not interfere in policies or problems which are distinctly American. George Meany must not interfere in problems which are definitely

Maritime Transportation Unions Canadian. This is a Canadian problem. It is a sordid one and we have to deal with it. I think the members of the Canadian Labour Congress and its executive council should be commended for the way they have wrestled with it and for the courageous decisions they have taken in connection with this matter.
I shall not bother to answer some of the charges which have been made in this house tonight and on other occasions against certain of the individuals concerned. Remarks have been made as to the position which Claude Jodoin took a couple of years ago. It was said that a couple of years ago he was defending Hal Banks. I myself was a member of the council four years ago when Claude Jodoin and the others expelled Hal Banks from the congress. As I say, I am not here to answer those allegations. They are answered by the facts. I believe those concerned are to be commended for having accepted this trusteeship, though only because it is absolutely necessary. I am asking tonight for two things. The first is that the government should cut down this five year provision, making it two or three years at the most. If the government wishes, let them make it possible to continue the trusteeship by resolution of both houses. Let it not go on and on automatically. Let us provide that as soon as the mess is cleared up it will be done away with. The situation which has arisen because of these statements from Washington is a serious one. I am fully confident that the officers of the C.L.C. will deal with their counterparts in Washington. I call on this government to deal with its counterpart in Washington, particularly with the issue raised by secretary of labour Wirtz.
Another thing I have to say is this. I regret that so many hon. members have sought to find a relationship between what is happening with regard to the imposition of this trusteeship and the strike on the St. Lawrence by the international longshoremen. I deplore the demands being made on the government for "big stick" action, demands which render no help in the settlement of that dispute. The thing that ought to be said-and this would really help the situation-is that there is not going to be compulsory arbitration. This is the place where a clear statement of that kind ought to be made. The workers are engaged, now, in a legal strike. It is up to the parties concerned to reach a settlement. The government has done its part by providing mediation, and the companies should know that they cannot, simply by dragging their feet, cause a situation where compulsory arbitration will be brought in, simply because of some of the things which have been said by the Leader of the Opposition.
There are five or six outstanding issues. One involves the payment of time and a half

for work done on Saturdays. Any employer in this year 1963 who refuses to grant time and a half for work on Saturdays is, surely, in an untenable position. Another thing the workers are demanding-or, at least, they were the last time I was informed-is pay for at least four hours of work when they are called in to work and there is nothing for them to do. This happens under present conditions on the St. Lawrence. Men are called to work at eight in the morning, but if when they get there there is no work for them to do they are sent home without a nickel of pay. The question of the wage rate has been more or less settled, and the men have given their executive officials power to deal with details of the kind I have mentioned. I suggest that what the companies and the shipping federation of Canada need to know is that this parliament believes in its own legislation- that it believes in free collective bargaining, and that parties to a dispute who have gone through the due processes of the law have the right to continue efforts to reach a settlement through mediation without threats of "the big stick" being used. The government, it is true, has not tried to wield a big stick, but the Leader of the Opposition has certainly suggested that it should. This is precisely what should not be done.
The imposition of a trusteeship on a gangster union, agreed to, because it is necessary, by four other unions which have a clean bill of health is a different thing from suggesting that a big stick should be used on a union which has complied with all the processes of the law and which is engaged in a legal strike, according to the Minister of Labour himself. Let us keep these two things separate. Let us go along with the Canadian Labour Congress. Let us cut down the period of time during which it is proposed the trusteeship should continue. Let us do all we can, with cool heads and understanding, to have the best possible relations we can with the United States in the trade union field, as in all others, for this is our only hope on this North American continent.

It had not been my intention to speak twice in the debate on this resolution. It was our intention that only three members of my party should speak on this occasion and we had hoped that the resolution would have passed through this house last evening.
However, that has not happened. Other hon. members have taken part in the debate on the resolution and in the course of the discussions certain allegations have been made, particularly by the hon. member for Greenwood and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, which oblige me to say a few brief words in respect to them. I hope the committee will allow me to complete my remarks, even if they go a few minutes beyond ten o'clock, so that we may be able to pass the resolution this evening. In any case it is necessary that I make some comments in respect to these allegations.
The hon. member for Kootenay West said this afternoon, if I heard him rightly, that there were certain people in this house who thought at one time that Mr. Banks was a good character. I think a number of these people must have been in the former Liberal government, because they thought so highly of Mr. Banks at that time that they sent him to Geneva, to the I.L.O. conference, to represent the Canadian labour movement.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Is it not a fact that the representatives sent by workers organizations to the I.L.O. are nominated by workers' organizations, in the same way as employers' representatives are nominated by employers' organizations, and that such nominations are usually accepted by any government?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
The Minister of Labour has answered his own question. Nominations are sent to the government and the minister of labour approves them. If he did not approve, then that representative would not represent labour. But in this instance the government thought enough of Mr. Banks that they felt that they should approve him as the right type to represent labour in Canada.
The allegation has been made that the government of the day and myself as minister did not perform our duties, and we have been charged with inaction with respect to the
Maritime Transportation Unions signing of two agreements, the agreements with the N.A.M.E. and the S.I.U. I do not mind the charge directed at me personally. After all, I have been in the political arena for some time and during my 11 years in this chamber, of which I am very proud, I have had many allegations made against me. When one is in politics he certainly learns how to take that sort of thing. But I do resent the allegations made against Mr. Bernard Wilson, the industrial relations officer, who is a very capable, sincere and experienced man in the labour department. The labour department is very fortunate to have him in their service; let me say that. He has been visited with the same charge as the government.
Anyone who is familiar with the whole history of the involved affairs of the N.A.M.E. and the S.I.U. knows the terrific confusion which developed because of successive officers of the N.A.M.E. who joined with Mr. Banks, until such time as they broke with him. The whole history of this matter is outlined in the report of Justice Norris, commencing at page 51. The fourth paragraph at page 51 says:
From the evidence, it appears that in 1954 and 1955 Banks seduced the executive of the great lakes and eastern district of the N.A.M.E._
Then the whole story of this confusion unfolds itself. All the time this was happening the S.I.U. was an affiliate of the Canadian Labour Congress.
This question was brought before the courts. Action was instituted by the N.A.M.E. in self-protection, but even the courts found it difficult to sort out the status of the N.A.M.E. During this time the Department of Labour and the Canada labour relations board took the position time and time again that the N.A.M.E. was a legally certified bargaining agent for the Canadian labour relations board, and I am sure hon. members know that the Canada labour relations board found that the
S.I.U. had gained control of the marine engineers by fraud. Mr. Norris refers to this on page 51, and on, in his report.
As far as my own responsibilities are concerned, I took all possible steps under these conditions to see that the marine engineers were protected. When a strike occurred over this situation I ordered Banks by telegram to get his men to resume work. I said in that telegram that if he wanted to represent the marine engineers he should make a proper application to the Canada labour relations board. Banks did this and several of the applications which he made to that board were rejected as fraud, as I have said. All this time I might point out that he was affiliated with the Canadian Labour Congress. Because of his raiding of the N.A.M.E. he

Maritime Transportation Unions and his union were thrown out of the Canadian Labour Congress. He was putting the ship owners, by threats and otherwise-
